items.q: A surgeon performs a primary total hip arthroplasty using the direct anterior (Hueter) approach. Which anatomical internervous plane is utilized during this approach?
o: Superficial between sartorius (femoral) and tensor fasciae latae (superior gluteal); deep between rectus femoris (femoral) and gluteus medius (superior gluteal)
Superficial between tensor fasciae latae and gluteus medius; deep between vastus lateralis and rectus femoris
Between gluteus medius (superior gluteal) and vastus lateralis (femoral)
Between gluteus maximus (inferior gluteal) and gluteus medius (superior gluteal)
items.e: The direct anterior (Smith-Petersen/Hueter) approach utilizes a true internervous plane. Superficial interval is between sartorius (femoral nerve) and tensor fasciae latae (superior gluteal nerve); the deep interval is between rectus femoris (femoral nerve) and gluteus medius (superior gluteal nerve).
items.note: Accurate anatomical internervous plane description, well-constructed distractors, directly tested in superspeciality exams.

items.q: According to the Wasielewski acetabular quadrant system for uncemented cup fixation, placing screws in the anterosuperior quadrant puts which major structures at immediate risk of injury?
o: Sciatic nerve and superior gluteal vessels
Inferior gluteal nerve and internal pudendal vessels
items.e: In the Wasielewski quadrant system, the anterosuperior quadrant of the acetabulum is designated as the 'death zone' because placing screws here risks injuring the external iliac artery and vein.
items.note: High-yield standard THA quadrant question, factually precise and accurate.

items.q: A 68-year-old male presents 3 years after a THA with sudden thigh pain after a low-energy fall. Radiographs reveal a femoral shaft fracture around the stem tip. Intraoperatively, the stem is tested and found to be well-fixed with stable mantle and adequate bone stock (Vancouver B1). What is the surgical management of choice?
o: Non-operative management with touch-down weight bearing in a hip spica
Open reduction and internal fixation with a locking plate and cables
Revision of the stem using a long tapered fluted modular stem
items.e: Vancouver B1 periprosthetic fractures occur around or just below a well-fixed stem with good bone stock. The standard management is open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) using a locking plate with cables (± strut allografts). Stem revision is reserved for loose stems (Vancouver B2/B3).
items.note: Classic exam scenario testing the Vancouver classification treatment algorithm.

items.q: Single-dose radiotherapy is selected for heterotopic ossification (HO) prophylaxis in a high-risk patient undergoing total hip arthroplasty. What is the standard recommended radiation dosage and administration window?
o: 15–20 Gy given within 12 hours before or 12 hours after surgery
7–8 Gy given within 24 hours before or 72 hours after surgery
2–4 Gy given within 48 hours before or 7 days after surgery
10–12 Gy given between 2 and 4 weeks postoperatively
items.e: For high-risk patients (e.g., ankylosing spondylitis, DISH, previous HO), single-dose radiotherapy of about 7–8 Gy administered within 24 hours before or 72 hours after surgery effectively prevents heterotopic ossification.
items.note: Standard board-level factual question on HO prophylaxis protocols.

items.q: During pre-operative templating for a total hip arthroplasty, the surgeon accurately plans the femoral offset. What clinical complication is most directly caused by an unintended reduction in femoral offset?
o: Trochanteric pain from excessive abductor tension
Abductor weakness and increased risk of impingement and dislocation
Peroneal nerve division sciatic palsy from soft tissue over-lengthening
items.e: Reducing femoral offset decreases soft tissue tension and shortens the abductor moment arm, leading to abductor weakness, increased risk of impingement, and dislocation. Excessive offset, conversely, causes trochanteric pain.
items.note: Core biomechanical concept in THA templating and execution.

items.q: In a direct lateral (Hardinge) approach to the hip joint, extending the proximal split in the gluteus medius muscle beyond what distance above the tip of the greater trochanter risks damaging the superior gluteal nerve?
items.e: In the direct lateral (Hardinge) transgluteal approach, splitting the gluteus medius more than about 5 cm proximal to the greater trochanter tip endangers the superior gluteal nerve, leading to abductor weakness and a postoperative Trendelenburg gait.
items.note: Classic anatomical anatomical distance high-yield fact for orthopaedic board exams.

items.q: A 62-year-old female presents 6 months after total hip arthroplasty with persistent anterior groin pain, specifically provoked by active resisted hip flexion. Radiographs demonstrate an acetabular cup that is prominent anteriorly. Which intervention is indicated for this condition?
o: Stem revision to a long-stem modular component
Iliopsoas tenotomy or acetabular cup revision
items.e: Anterior cup prominence causing groin pain during resisted hip flexion indicates iliopsoas impingement. Treatment options include iliopsoas tenotomy or acetabular cup revision.
items.note: Clear clinical vignette describing iliopsoas impingement post-THA.

items.q: For successful bone ingrowth into an uncemented porous-coated femoral component, what is the required optimal pore size and maximum allowable interface micromotion?
o: Pore size 100–400 microns; micromotion under about 40–150 microns
Pore size 10–50 microns; micromotion under about 500–600 microns
Pore size 500–1000 microns; micromotion under about 10–20 microns
Pore size 1–5 microns; micromotion under about 200–300 microns
items.e: Fixation of uncemented stems via osseous ingrowth requires an optimal porous coating pore size of 100–400 microns and initial interface micromotion under about 40–150 microns.
items.note: Standard basic science / implant fixation question with precise numerical parameters.

items.q: A surgeon is performing a primary total knee arthroplasty using the Mechanical Alignment (MA) philosophy. Which of the following principles accurately describes the distal femoral and proximal tibial bone cuts in this approach?
o: Both femoral and tibial cuts are made perpendicular to their respective mechanical axes
The tibial cut is made in 3 degrees varus while the femoral cut is in neutral alignment
The femoral and tibial cuts are performed parallel to the native anatomical axes
Implants are positioned within native pre-arthritic alignment without soft-tissue releases
items.e: In mechanical alignment (MA), both the distal femoral cut and proximal tibial cut are made strictly perpendicular to their respective mechanical axes. Soft-tissue releases are then performed as needed to achieve equal flexion and extension gaps.
items.note: Accurate, clear single-best answer fully supported by standard orthopaedic principles and reference notes.

items.q: A 64-year-old female presents with severe anterior knee pain, patellar tilt, and lateral subluxation 1 year after undergoing primary total knee arthroplasty. Infection and loosening have been ruled out. Which of the following imaging modalities is the investigation of choice to evaluate for component malrotation?
items.e: Combined internal rotation of the femoral or tibial component causes patellar maltracking, lateral subluxation, anterior knee pain, patellar complications, and stiffness. Computed Tomography (CT) is the investigation of choice to accurately quantify femoral and tibial component rotation.
items.note: High-yield standard question with CT as the definitive answer.

items.q: During a primary total knee arthroplasty using the gap-balancing technique, trial evaluation after initial bone cuts reveals that the knee is tight in extension but balanced and stable in flexion. What is the most appropriate step to correct this gap mismatch?
o: Release posterior capsule and osteophytes, then resect additional distal femur
Downsize the femoral component using an anterior referencing guide
Increase the posterior slope of the tibial component
items.e: When the knee is tight in extension but balanced in flexion, the extension gap must be selectively widened. This is accomplished by releasing the posterior capsule and posterior osteophytes, followed by additional distal femoral resection (~2 mm) if tightness persists.
items.note: Classic TKA gap balancing algorithm question, fully accurate.

items.q: During soft-tissue balancing for a severe valgus knee deformity in total knee arthroplasty, which of the following tight lateral structures is contracted selectively in flexion?
items.e: In a valgus knee, the iliotibial band (ITB) and posterolateral capsule are tight in extension, the lateral collateral ligament (LCL) is tight in both flexion and extension, whereas the popliteus tendon is tight predominantly in flexion.
items.note: Directly supported by Campbell's and reference notes; tests high-yield anatomical concepts.

items.q: A patient undergoes total knee arthroplasty for correction of a severe fixed valgus deformity with a concomitant flexion contracture. In the recovery room, the patient develops signs of acute peroneal nerve palsy. What is the recommended immediate initial management?
o: Flex the knee and loosen all compressive dressings
Place the limb in a rigid extension splint
Immediate surgical exploration and decompression of the nerve in the popliteal fossa
Revise the prosthesis to a constrained rotating-hinge design
items.e: Peroneal nerve palsy following correction of a severe valgus and flexion contracture occurs due to nerve traction. The immediate initial management is to flex the knee and loosen all dressings. Surgical exploration is reserved for cases that fail to recover.
items.note: Standard board question on post-TKA nerve palsy management.

items.q: Anterior femoral cortex notching during distal femoral preparation in total knee arthroplasty increases the risk of early periprosthetic fracture. By approximately how much does anterior notching reduce the torsional strength of the distal femur?
items.e: Anterior femoral cortex notching significantly weakens the structural integrity of the distal femur, reducing its torsional strength by approximately 30–40% and substantially predisposing the patient to supracondylar periprosthetic fractures.
items.note: Standard fact-based question with exact biomechanical values established in literature.

items.q: During medial soft-tissue balancing for a fixed varus knee deformity in total knee arthroplasty, which step should be performed FIRST before formal ligamentous releases?
o: Subperiosteal release of the superficial MCL
Release of the deep MCL (meniscotibial ligament)
Removal of medial tibial and femoral osteophytes
Pie-crusting of the anterior fibers of the superficial MCL
items.e: Medial soft-tissue balancing in a varus knee begins with complete removal of medial tibial and femoral osteophytes. Osteophytes tent the soft-tissue sleeve; removing them restores native tissue length and often reduces tightness prior to structural ligament releases.
items.note: Fundamental step in varus knee TKA technique, highly exam-relevant.

items.q: Which of the following clinical scenarios represents an absolute indication for choosing a linked rotating-hinge total knee prosthesis over unconstrained or non-linked constrained designs?
o: Neuromuscular recurvatum deformity with global ligamentous deficiency
Isolated absence of the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL)
Inflammatory arthritis with intact collateral ligaments
Tightness in extension with normal flexion gap stability
items.e: A linked rotating-hinge prosthesis provides total mechanical constraint and is indicated in cases of global ligamentous deficiency, severe bone loss, hyperextension instability, or neuromuscular recurvatum (such as post-polio syndrome). Isolated PCL loss is managed with a posterior-stabilised (PS) implant.
items.note: Clear absolute indication for highest degree of implant constraint.

items.q: Regarding surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis for total joint arthroplasty to prevent periprosthetic joint infection, which of the following statements is correct based on standard guidelines?
o: Cefazolin should be administered within 120 minutes prior to skin incision
Vancomycin should be administered within 120 minutes prior to incision in MRSA-colonized patients
Prophylactic antibiotics should be routinely continued for 72 hours postoperatively
Redosing of prophylactic cefazolin is recommended after 2 hours of operative time
items.e: Vancomycin should be administered within 120 minutes prior to skin incision in patients colonized with MRSA or with beta-lactam allergy, whereas cefazolin is given within 60 minutes. Cefazolin redosing is indicated after about 4 hours (or blood loss > 1,500 mL), and prophylactic antibiotics should be discontinued within 24 hours.
items.note: Standard antimicrobial prophylaxis guidelines correctly queried.

items.q: A 65-year-old woman develops acute right hip pain and fever 2 years after THA, with symptoms present for 4 days (acute haematogenous infection). Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus and radiographs show well-fixed components. If debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention (DAIR) is undertaken, which intraoperative step is mandatory?
o: Retention of all original components without modular exchange
Placement of a static antibiotic-loaded cement spacer
Exchange of all modular components including head and polyethylene liner
Removal of the femoral stem while retaining the acetabular cup
items.e: Exchange of all modular components (head and liner/polyethylene insert) is an essential element of DAIR. It allows access for thorough debridement of the interface beneath modular components and improves infection eradication.
items.note: Essential surgical step of DAIR protocol is correctly identified.

items.q: Under the Tsukayama classification for periprosthetic joint infection, an infection presenting within the first month after primary joint arthroplasty is categorized as:
items.e: The Tsukayama classification categorizes early post-operative periprosthetic joint infection occurring within the first month (4 weeks) as Type 1. Type 2 is late chronic (>1 month), Type 3 is acute haematogenous, and Type 4 is unexpected positive intraoperative cultures at revision.
items.note: Standard Tsukayama classification definition perfectly matched.

items.q: Which of the following trial results regarding antibiotic management of periprosthetic joint infection is correct?
o: The OVIVA trial showed intravenous antibiotic therapy is superior to oral therapy during the first 6 weeks
The DATIPO trial demonstrated that 12 weeks of antibiotics is superior to 6 weeks for PJI treatment
The DATIPO trial concluded that 6 weeks of antibiotic treatment has lower recurrence rates than 12 weeks
The OVIVA trial recommended intravenous therapy for a minimum of 12 weeks for all PJI cases
items.e: The DATIPO trial (2021) demonstrated that 12 weeks of antibiotic therapy was superior to 6 weeks for PJI in persistent infection rates. The OVIVA trial (2019) showed that oral antibiotics were non-inferior to intravenous antibiotics within the first 6 weeks.
items.note: High-yield landmark RCT findings accurately stated.

items.q: When evaluating an inconclusive preoperative score (2 to 5 points) using the 2018 ICM definition for periprosthetic joint infection, which intraoperative finding awards 3 points toward the diagnostic score?
o: A single positive intraoperative tissue culture
items.e: In the 2018 ICM intraoperative criteria for inconclusive cases, intraoperative gross purulence and positive histology (>5 neutrophils/HPF in 5 or more fields) each award 3 points. A single positive culture awards 2 points.
items.note: Accurate application of 2018 ICM intraoperative scoring system.

items.q: Before performing a diagnostic joint aspiration for suspected chronic periprosthetic joint infection, antimicrobial therapy should ideally be withheld for at least:
items.e: To maximize culture yield and avoid false-negative synovial cultures, antibiotics should be stopped for at least 2 weeks prior to performing joint aspiration in suspected PJI.
items.note: Standard workup protocol supported by ICM and AAOS guidelines.

items.q: A hip arthroplasty surgeon is evaluating post-irradiation thermal processing options for highly cross-linked polyethylene (HXLPE). What is the primary drawback of thermal remelting (heating above the melting point of ~135–137 °C) compared to annealing?
o: Persistence of high levels of unquenched free radicals causing early oxidation
Reduction in crystallinity, fatigue strength, and fracture toughness
Complete loss of wear resistance improvements achieved by cross-linking
Increased production of submicron bioactive wear particles
items.e: Thermal remelting above the melting point eliminates free radicals completely but reduces polymer crystallinity, fatigue strength, and fracture toughness. In contrast, thermal annealing below the melting point preserves mechanical properties but leaves residual free radicals prone to in-vivo oxidation.
items.note: Accurate, well-constructed question testing a high-yield concept directly supported by reference notes.

items.q: A 68-year-old male who underwent total hip arthroplasty 15 years ago presents with severe groin pain and limb shortening. Radiographs reveal severe eccentric liner wear with complete wear-through of the polyethylene, resulting in direct articulation of the cobalt-chromium femoral head against the titanium acetabular shell. According to McKellop's classification, which mode of wear is taking place?
items.e: McKellop Mode 2 wear refers to an intended primary surface rubbing against a non-intended secondary surface, such as the femoral head eroding through the liner and wearing directly against the metallic acetabular shell. Mode 1 is intended bearing surfaces, Mode 3 is third-body particles between primary surfaces, and Mode 4 is two non-intended surfaces rubbing together.
items.note: Factually accurate and classic classification question directly matching standard arthroplasty guidelines.

items.q: A patient with a ceramic-on-ceramic total hip arthroplasty sustains a ceramic femoral head fracture after a fall. Intraoperatively, extensive synovectomy is performed, and minor scratching of the stem trunnion is noted. Which of the following is the most appropriate step regarding femoral head replacement?
o: Implant a cobalt-chromium femoral head directly onto the scratched stem trunnion
Implant a new ceramic femoral head using a titanium adapter taper sleeve over the trunnion
Implant a stainless steel head without a sleeve to minimize wear debris
Perform a resection arthroplasty as component revision is contraindicated
items.e: When revising a fractured ceramic head, a new ceramic head must be used (often with a titanium taper sleeve if the trunnion has damage). A metallic head should never be used because retained third-body ceramic particles in the joint space will cause rapid, catastrophic wear of a metal head.
items.note: Standard board-level question with complete accuracy based on standard arthroplasty guidelines.

items.q: A 62-year-old male with a metal-on-polyethylene total hip arthroplasty incorporating a 36-mm cobalt-chromium head presents with groin discomfort. Serum ion analysis demonstrates an elevated cobalt level of 12 µg/L and a chromium level of 2.5 µg/L (cobalt-to-chromium ratio > 4). MARS MRI reveals a pericapsular fluid collection without component loosening. What is the primary underlying cause of these findings?
o: Adhesive wear of the highly cross-linked polyethylene liner
Mechanically assisted crevice corrosion at the head-neck taper junction
Delamination wear of the acetabular liner due to insufficient thickness
Third-body wear from embedded polymethylmethacrylate cement fragments
items.e: Mechanically assisted crevice corrosion (trunnionosis) at the modular head-neck junction releases predominantly cobalt relative to chromium, leading to a high Co:Cr ratio (> 3–5) and adverse local tissue reactions (ALTR) even in metal-on-polyethylene bearings. Bearing surface wear in MoM typically elevates both cobalt and chromium more symmetrically.
items.note: High-yield clinical scenario accurately testing trunnionosis diagnosis via serum ion ratio.

items.q: Polyethylene wear debris induces osteolysis through macrophage activation and subsequent osteoclastogenesis. Which particle size range of ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene is recognized as the most bioactive in triggering this inflammatory cascade?
items.e: Polyethylene wear particles in the 0.1 to 1 micron size range are the most bioactive. They are readily phagocytosed by macrophages, triggering the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, PGE2) and upregulating RANKL to stimulate osteoclastic bone resorption.
items.note: Factually precise question on the fundamental mechanism of wear-particle-induced osteolysis.

items.q: Which of the following statements regarding bearing material properties and tribology in joint replacement is correct?
o: Titanium alloy is an ideal femoral head bearing surface due to superior scratch resistance
Titanium is never used as an articulating bearing surface because of its poor wear resistance
Cobalt-chromium alloy has higher surface hardness and scratch resistance than alumina ceramic
Ceramic bearings rely exclusively on boundary lubrication due to poor fluid surface wettability
items.e: Titanium alloy has poor wear resistance and high notch sensitivity, so it is never used as an articulating bearing surface in joint arthroplasty. Ceramics have the highest hardness and excellent wettability (hydrophilicity), enabling fluid-film lubrication.
items.note: Unambiguous tribology question testing standard properties of arthroplasty materials.

items.q: A joint replacement surgeon is evaluating candidates for metal-on-metal Birmingham Hip Resurfacing (BHR). Based on risk factors for adverse local tissue reactions and early failure, which patient is the most suitable candidate?
o: A 45-year-old male with primary osteoarthritis, a large femoral head, and good bone quality
A 68-year-old postmenopausal female with severe osteoporosis and small femoral head size
A 40-year-old female with developmental dysplasia of the hip and severe acetabular dysplasia
A 52-year-old male with chronic renal impairment and avascular necrosis with large femoral head cysts
items.e: Hip resurfacing produces optimal long-term results in young, active males with large femoral heads and normal bone density. Female sex, small component size, osteoporosis, large femoral head cysts, AVN, DDH, and renal impairment are major contraindications due to high failure and ALTR rates.
items.note: Clear and clinically accurate question assessing indications and contraindications for hip resurfacing.

items.q: Wear in total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is primarily fatigue-dominated (delamination and pitting) due to low conformity and high contact stresses. What is the minimum recommended polyethylene liner thickness required in TKA to reduce subsurface fatigue failures?
items.e: Polyethylene thickness in total knee arthroplasty should be at least 6–8 mm. Thinner inserts result in excessive contact stress within the subsurface material, dramatically increasing the risk of fatigue wear mechanisms such as delamination and pitting.
items.note: Direct, standard superspeciality entrance exam question with clear numerical cut-off.

items.q: A 68-year-old male undergoing revision THA for aseptic loosening has radiographical evidence of extensive metaphyseal bone loss with non-supportive metaphysis, but has 2.5 cm of intact diaphysis at the isthmus. According to the Paprosky femoral classification, which category does this represent, and what implant design is indicated?
o: Paprosky Type IIIA; Extensively porous-coated cylindrical stem
Paprosky Type IIIB; Modular tapered fluted titanium stem
Paprosky Type II; Primary cemented stem
Paprosky Type IV; Proximal femoral replacement
items.e: Paprosky Type IIIB femoral bone loss is defined by a non-supportive metaphysis with less than 4 cm of intact diaphyseal isthmus support. The reconstruction of choice for Type IIIB defects is a modular tapered fluted titanium stem to achieve distal diaphyseal fixation.
items.note: Accurate, clear single-best answer, supported by reference notes.

items.q: During revision total knee arthroplasty for severe arthrofibrosis, standard medial parapatellar arthrotomy provides inadequate exposure. To protect against patellar tendon avulsion, which exposure extension maneuver is recommended as the initial procedure of choice?
o: Patellar tendon release from tibial tubercle
items.e: The quadriceps snip (a proximal oblique incision across the quadriceps tendon) is the first-line exposure extension maneuver during revision TKA because it provides safe exposure without requiring special post-operative rehabilitation modifications or causing significant extensor lag.
items.note: Accurate and directly supported by standard revision TKA surgical principles.

items.q: A 74-year-old female presents with severe groin pain 12 years after total hip arthroplasty. Preoperative radiographs reveal superior acetabular component migration of over 3 cm, greater than 60% loss of acetabular rim, non-supportive columns, severe ischial lysis, and a broken Kohler line with medial translation of the hemipelvis. Which Paprosky acetabular classification is assigned?
items.e: Paprosky Type IIIB ('up and in') defects are characterized by greater than 60% acetabular rim loss, non-supportive columns, superior migration greater than 3 cm, severe ischial lysis, and destruction of the Kohler line, often associated with pelvic discontinuity.
items.note: Completely accurate Paprosky acetabular classification question supported by reference notes.

items.q: According to the Harris criteria for evaluating component loosening of a cemented femoral stem in revision total hip arthroplasty, which of the following is classified as 'definite' loosening?
o: Radiolucent line involving 50% to 100% of the bone-cement interface
Continuous radiolucent line around the entire cement mantle
Migration of the femoral stem, cement fracture, or stem fracture
Non-progressive 1 mm radiolucency restricted to Zone 1
items.e: The Harris criteria define 'definite' loosening of a cemented femoral stem as stem migration relative to the cement mantle, fracture of the cement mantle, or fracture of the stem component itself. A continuous radiolucent line surrounding the entire cement mantle is classified as 'probable' loosening.
items.note: Factually correct standard criteria question, directly aligned with reference notes.

items.q: During revision total knee arthroplasty, significant tibial bone loss is identified involving both the medial and lateral plateaus (AORI Type 2B). Based on the Morgan-Jones three-zone fixation principles, predictable construct stability requires solid fixation in at least how many zones?
items.e: The Morgan-Jones three-zone fixation principles divide the knee into three zones: Zone 1 (epiphysis), Zone 2 (metaphysis), and Zone 3 (diaphysis). The gold standard requirement for reliable long-term revision construct stability is achieving solid mechanical fixation in at least two of the three zones.
items.note: Accurate, high-yield concept directly supported by text.

items.q: According to joint registry data and revision arthroplasty principles, which of the following correctly pairs the most common cause of early revision (< 2 years) in TKA with the most common long-term cause of failure in THA?
o: Early TKA: Infection; Long-term THA: Aseptic loosening/osteolysis
Early TKA: Aseptic loosening; Long-term THA: Dislocation
Early TKA: Periprosthetic fracture; Long-term THA: Infection
Early TKA: Arthrofibrosis; Long-term THA: Adverse reaction to metal debris
items.e: Periprosthetic joint infection is the single most common cause of early TKA failure (within 2 years of index surgery), whereas aseptic loosening and osteolysis represent the most common long-term failure mechanism leading to revision THA.
items.note: Standard epidemiology facts fully supported by arthroplasty registries and reference notes.

items.q: A 65-year-old male presents with start-up thigh pain 5 years after an uncemented THA. Serial radiographs demonstrate progressive lucency around the proximal stem and distal endosteal bone bridging around the un-ingrown tip of the stem. Which radiographical feature is described, and what does it indicate regarding stem stability?
o: Spot weld, indicating stable osseous ingrowth
Stress shielding, indicating stable fibrous fixation
Heterotopic ossification, indicating stable mechanical anchorage
items.e: Start-up thigh pain is a classic clinical indicator of femoral stem loosening. Endosteal bone formation bridging the canal around the tip of an uncemented stem is termed a 'pedestal,' which signifies distal mechanical abutment of a loose femoral component lacking proximal bony ingrowth.
items.note: Factually precise radiographical descriptor and interpretation supported by reference notes.

items.q: A 64-year-old man with primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis undergoes axial CT scanning of the shoulder. The scan demonstrates posterior glenoid bone loss with a monoconcave glenoid surface, posterior humeral head subluxation, and glenoid retroversion of 18 degrees. According to the Walch classification, how is this glenoid morphology categorized?
items.e: Walch B3 is characterized by a monoconcave glenoid surface with posterior bone loss, posterior subluxation, and retroversion over 15 degrees. In contrast, Walch B2 represents a biconcave glenoid, and Walch C indicates a dysplastic glenoid with retroversion exceeding 25 degrees.
items.note: Accurate, well-constructed question based on the updated Walch classification.

items.q: Scapular notching is the most common radiological finding following reverse total shoulder arthroplasty (RTSA). Which of the following technical or design modifications helps to reduce the risk of inferior scapular notching?
o: Using a humeral stem design with a lower neck-shaft angle (135–145 degrees)
Superior placement of the glenosphere on the glenoid
Superior tilting of the glenoid baseplate
Decreasing the diameter of the glenosphere
items.e: Modern RTSA designs reduce scapular notching by using lower neck-shaft angles (135–145 degrees), inferior glenosphere placement, inferior tilt of the baseplate, lateralization, or a larger glenosphere.
items.note: Factually precise biomechanical question on RTSA design parameters.

items.q: A 62-year-old man develops persistent deep pain 10 months after an anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty. diagnostic joint aspiration is performed for suspected periprosthetic joint infection (PJI). Given the most common causative organism implicated in shoulder PJI, how long should intraoperative tissue cultures be held in the microbiology laboratory?
items.e: Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes is the most common pathogen in shoulder PJI. Because it is a slow-growing organism, tissue cultures must be held for 14 days to properly detect it.
items.note: Standard high-yield exam question testing shoulder PJI protocol.

items.q: A 74-year-old woman undergoes reverse total shoulder arthroplasty (RTSA). She initially achieves active forward elevation of 130 degrees. At 3 months postoperatively, she experiences sudden posterior shoulder pain and loss of elevation. Radiographs show a stress fracture at the base of the acromion involving the scapular spine origin of the deltoid. According to the Levy classification, this fracture is categorized as:
items.e: The Levy classification categorizes acromial and scapular spine stress fractures following RTSA into Type 1 (acromion tip), Type 2 (base of the acromion or scapular spine origin of the deltoid), and Type 3 (scapular spine).
items.note: Clear, single-best-answer classification question directly from Campbell's.

items.q: When evaluating a complex proximal humerus fracture using the Hertel (LEGO) criteria, which of the following combinations indicates the highest risk of post-traumatic humeral head ischemia?
o: Metaphyseal head extension > 8 mm and intact medial hinge
Metaphyseal head extension > 8 mm and anatomical neck fracture pattern
Intact medial hinge (< 2 mm displacement) and metaphyseal head extension > 8 mm
Metaphyseal head extension < 8 mm and disrupted medial hinge (> 2 mm displacement)
items.e: The Hertel criteria predict humeral head ischemia based on metaphyseal head extension under 8 mm, disrupted medial hinge (over 2 mm displacement), and an anatomical neck fracture pattern.
items.note: Classic criteria question with accurate distractors.

items.q: A 70-year-old patient presents with cuff tear arthropathy and severe anterosuperior humeral head escape due to loss of the coracoacromial arch (Seebauer type IIB). Why is performing a concomitant acromioplasty or coracoacromial (CA) ligament release contraindicated in this setting?
o: It causes catastrophic anterosuperior escape of the humeral head
It impairs the origin of the teres minor muscle
It leads to direct injury of the axillary nerve
It prevents deltoid tensioning required for reverse shoulder arthroplasty
items.e: In decentred cuff tear arthropathy with coracoacromial arch deficiency (Seebauer IIB), the CA ligament acts as a key secondary restraint against anterosuperior escape. Releasing it leads to catastrophic anterosuperior instability.
items.note: High-yield clinical surgical concept question.

items.q: A 72-year-old patient undergoing reverse total shoulder arthroplasty (RTSA) exhibits severe loss of active external rotation with a positive Hornblower's sign (external rotation lag) due to complete dysfunction of the teres minor. Which co-procedure at the time of RTSA is indicated to restore active external rotation?
o: Latissimus dorsi (± teres major) tendon transfer
items.e: Active external rotation after RTSA relies heavily on the teres minor. In its absence (positive Hornblower's sign), a latissimus dorsi (± teres major) tendon transfer (L'Episcopo-type) combined with RTSA is indicated.
items.note: Standard subspecialty surgical indication question.

items.q: A 66-year-old woman who underwent anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty via a deltopectoral approach 6 months ago presents with anterior shoulder instability and weakness in internal rotation. Which physical examination maneuver is most appropriate to evaluate for failure of the subscapularis repair?
items.e: Subscapularis failure after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty presents with internal rotation weakness and anterior instability. It is evaluated clinically using the belly-press test and the lift-off test.
items.note: Direct clinical question testing physical exam of a common post-TSA complication.

items.q: Which of the following conditions is considered an absolute contraindication for fixed-bearing medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) according to classical Kozinn and Scott criteria?
o: Outerbridge grade II chondromalacia of the patellofemoral joint
Absence of a functional anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)
items.e: Absence of a functional ACL is an absolute contraindication for UKA because anteromedial instability leads to abnormal kinematics, posterior subluxation of the tibia, and rapid failure of the implant. Mild patellofemoral chondromalacia without severe grooving or retropatellar pain is not a contraindication.
items.note: Accurate, classical guideline question commonly tested in orthopaedic superspeciality exams.

items.q: On a full-length weight-bearing lower limb radiograph after a medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy (HTO) for medial compartment osteoarthritis, what is the ideal target position of the mechanical axis line across the tibial plateau?
o: 50% of the tibial width (center of the knee joint)
80% to 85% of the tibial width measured from the medial border
35% to 40% of the tibial width measured from the medial border
62% to 65% of the tibial width measured from the medial border
items.e: The ideal target for mechanical axis correction during HTO for medial compartment OA is the Fujisawa point, which is 62% to 65% of the total tibial plateau width measured from the medial edge. This slight overcorrection into valgus unloads the degenerate medial compartment while avoiding excessive lateral compartment overload.
items.note: Standard high-yield point on mechanical alignment targets in HTO.

items.q: A 50-year-old active male presents with symptomatic lateral compartment osteoarthritis of the knee and a 12-degree valgus deformity. Preoperative full-length standing radiographs demonstrate an abnormal lateral distal femoral angle (LDFA < 85 degrees) with a normal medial proximal tibial angle (MPTA). Which osteotomy is the procedure of choice?
items.e: When a valgus deformity originates primarily from the distal femur (decreased LDFA), correction should be performed at the site of deformity using a distal femoral osteotomy (DFO), classically via a medial closing-wedge or lateral opening-wedge technique. Performing high tibial osteotomy in this setting would result in an oblique, tilted joint line.
items.note: Classic management principles for extra-articular femoral versus tibial deformities in knee joint preservation.

items.q: Unless specific technical modifications are made during surgical execution, a standard medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy (HTO) inherently causes which of the following changes to knee anatomy?
o: Increased posterior tibial slope and patella baja
Decreased posterior tibial slope and patella alta
Increased posterior tibial slope and patella alta
Decreased posterior tibial slope and patella baja
items.e: Medial opening-wedge HTO inherently increases the posterior tibial slope because the osteotomy gap tends to open wider anteriorly than posteriorly. Additionally, opening the wedge proximal to the tibial tubercle elevates the joint line relative to the patella, resulting in pseudo-patella baja.
items.note: Standard biomechanical and technical principle described in Campbell's and Miller's.

items.q: A 65-year-old female undergoes unicompartmental knee arthroplasty. Six months postoperatively, she experiences a sudden painful click while flexing her knee, followed by an inability to fully extend the joint. Radiographs show displacement of the polyethylene insert out of the joint space. This specific complication occurs in which type of knee arthroplasty?
items.e: Polyethylene bearing dislocation is a unique complication of mobile-bearing UKA (such as the Oxford knee), typically caused by surgical malalignment, soft-tissue imbalance, or gap asymmetry. Fixed-bearing implants have the polyethylene locked to the metal tray and cannot dislocate in this manner.
items.note: Clear distinction between mobile-bearing and fixed-bearing UKA complications.

items.q: During a medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy, an intra-articular fracture extending into the lateral tibial plateau (Takeuchi Type I lateral hinge fracture) is most commonly caused by which technical error?
o: Placing the osteotomy hinge point too distal (more than 2 cm below the lateral joint line)
Failing to perform a fibular osteotomy in all patients
Placing the osteotomy hinge point too proximal (less than 5 mm below the lateral joint line)
Making the distal cut complete through the lateral periosteum
items.e: Takeuchi Type I hinge fractures are intra-articular fractures extending into the lateral tibial plateau. They occur when the lateral cortical hinge is placed too superiorly (less than 5–10 mm below the lateral joint line) or when the osteotomy wedge is opened forcefully without adequate hinge relief.
items.note: Standard classification (Takeuchi) and intraoperative complication analysis in HTO.

items.q: A 42-year-old athlete with chronic anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) deficiency and early medial compartment varus osteoarthritis undergoes high tibial osteotomy. To decrease resting strain on an ACL graft during simultaneous or staged reconstruction, how should the posterior tibial slope be adjusted?
o: Slope changes do not affect ACL tension
items.e: Decreasing the posterior tibial slope reduces anterior tibial translation during weight-bearing, thereby reducing strain on the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). Conversely, increasing the posterior tibial slope increases anterior tibial shear and increases ACL strain.
items.note: Well-established biomechanical concept tested in subspecialty exams.

items.q: During the posterior tibial transverse osteotomy cut of a high tibial osteotomy, which major vascular structure is directly at risk if protective retractors are not properly placed deep to the popliteus muscle against the posterior cortex?
items.e: The popliteal artery lies directly behind the posterior surface of the proximal tibia, separated primarily by the popliteus muscle. Careful placement of a protective subperiosteal retractor directly against the posterior tibial cortex during the posterior cut of an HTO is essential to avoid laceration or pseudoaneurysm formation.
items.note: Crucial surgical anatomy fact in HTO procedures.

items.q: During an anatomic ACL reconstruction, which osseous landmark is used to specifically separate the footprints of the anteromedial (AM) and posterolateral (PL) bundles on the medial wall of the lateral femoral condyle?
items.e: The lateral bifurcate ridge separates the AM and PL bundle footprints. The lateral intercondylar ridge (also known as Resident's ridge) marks the anterior/superior limit of the ACL footprint.
items.note: Correct anatomical landmark as per Campbell's and the provided notes.

items.q: A 24-year-old professional footballer undergoes ACL reconstruction. Which of the following is the most sensitive physical examination finding for detecting an ACL deficiency in the acute setting?
items.e: The Lachman test is the most sensitive test for ACL rupture. The pivot shift is the most specific but is often difficult to perform in acute settings due to pain and guarding, being best performed under anaesthesia.
items.note: Standard clinical sensitivity/specificity facts for ACL examination.

items.q: Regarding the outcomes of the KANON trial (Frobell et al.) for acute ACL tears in young active adults, which statement is correct?
o: Early reconstruction resulted in significantly better 5-year outcomes compared to rehabilitation.
Approximately 50% of patients managed with initial rehabilitation avoided surgery and had similar 5-year outcomes.
Delayed reconstruction led to a 90% rate of secondary osteoarthritis at 2 years.
Immediate surgery is mandatory to prevent all future meniscal injuries.
items.e: The KANON trial demonstrated that a strategy of rehabilitation with the option of delayed reconstruction resulted in similar outcomes to early reconstruction at 2 and 5 years, with about half of the rehabilitation group avoiding surgery.
items.note: Accurately reflects the landmark KANON trial results mentioned in the reference notes.

items.q: A patient presents with knee instability. On examination, there is increased external rotation (positive dial test) at 30 degrees of flexion, but the asymmetry is no longer present when tested at 90 degrees of flexion. This finding specifically indicates an injury to the:
items.e: A positive dial test (over 10 degrees asymmetry) at 30 degrees of flexion only is characteristic of an isolated PLC injury. If it is positive at both 30 and 90 degrees, it suggests a combined PCL and PLC injury.
items.note: Classic clinical diagnostic algorithm for PLC vs combined PCL/PLC injuries.

items.q: A 30-year-old patient who underwent ACL reconstruction 6 months ago presents with a lack of terminal extension and a 'clunk' sensation during the final few degrees of straightening the knee. MRI shows a fibroproliferative nodule anterior to the graft. What is the most likely cause?
items.e: A cyclops lesion is a fibroproliferative nodule that forms anterior to the graft, often associated with a tibial tunnel placed too anteriorly (causing roof impingement). It typically presents with a loss of terminal extension and a 'clunk'.
items.note: Classic presentation and MRI findings of a cyclops lesion.

items.q: In a patient with a PCL injury, the examiner performs a posterior drawer test and finds that the tibia is flush with the femoral condyles (loss of the normal 1 cm anterior step-off). This corresponds to which grade of PCL injury?
items.e: Grade I is 0-5 mm translation (tibia still anterior to condyles). Grade II is 5-10 mm translation (tibia flush with condyles). Grade III is >10 mm translation (tibia posterior to condyles), which often suggests a combined injury.
items.note: Standard PCL injury grading based on tibial step-off.

items.q: Which of the following technical errors during ACL reconstruction is most likely to result in a graft that is tight in flexion, leading to restricted range of motion?
o: Femoral tunnel placed too low (at 4 o'clock position)
items.e: Placing the femoral tunnel too anteriorly is the most common technical error; it causes the graft to tighten excessively during flexion, leading to loss of flexion or graft failure. An anterior tibial tunnel causes impingement in extension.
items.note: Common technical error and its biomechanical consequence as described in Campbell's.

items.q: A 40-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a high-energy knee dislocation. Following successful reduction, distal pulses are present and equal. The Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) is measured as 0.82. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Admission for serial clinical observation only
Immediate ligamentous repair of all torn structures
CT angiography or formal vascular consultation
items.e: In knee dislocations, an ABI < 0.9 is highly suspicious for popliteal artery injury, even if pulses are palpable. These patients require further vascular evaluation, such as CT angiography.
items.note: Standard trauma protocol for vascular assessment in knee dislocations.

items.q: A 22-year-old athlete sustains a radial tear of the lateral meniscus. Biomechanically, why is this specific tear pattern considered functionally equivalent to a total meniscectomy?
o: It disrupts the random superficial collagen mesh
It transects the circumferential fibers, abolishing hoop stress function
It involves the type II collagen fibers in the white-white zone
It prevents the popliteus tendon from providing secondary stability
items.e: Circumferential fibers are the dominant deep fibers that convert axial loads into hoop stresses; radial tears transect these fibers, leading to a complete loss of meniscal load-bearing function, similar to a total meniscectomy or a root tear.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the biomechanical role of circumferential fibers and the impact of radial tears as described in the reference notes.

items.q: An 18-year-old footballer undergoes arthroscopic repair of a longitudinal medial meniscal tear located 2 mm from the meniscocapsular junction. Which of the following is true regarding this injury?
o: It is in the white-white zone and unlikely to heal
It is in the red-red zone with good healing potential
It is in the red-white zone with moderate healing potential
Vascularity in this region is provided by the middle genicular artery only
items.e: In adults, the peripheral 10-30% of the meniscus is vascular (perimeniscal capillary plexus). The 'red-red' zone is defined as the region within 3 mm of the periphery and has the best healing potential.
items.note: The classification of vascular zones and the specific distance (2 mm) correctly identify the red-red zone according to the provided notes.

items.q: A 52-year-old patient presents with medial joint line pain and a horizontal cleavage tear of the medial meniscus on MRI, without mechanical locking. Radiographs show Grade 1-2 osteoarthritic changes. Based on the FIDELITY and METEOR trials, what is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Inside-out repair with vertical mattress sutures
items.e: Large trials like FIDELITY and MeTeOR have demonstrated that arthroscopic partial meniscectomy (APM) is no more effective than physiotherapy or sham surgery for degenerative meniscal tears in middle-aged patients without true mechanical locking.
items.note: The question correctly applies the evidence-based management of degenerative meniscal tears as cited in the reference notes.

items.q: Which of the following biochemical changes correctly distinguishes osteoarthritic cartilage from healthy aging cartilage?
o: Water content increases in early osteoarthritis but decreases in aging
Keratan sulphate concentration increases in osteoarthritis
The modulus of elasticity increases in osteoarthritis
Chondroitin sulphate levels decrease in osteoarthritis
items.e: In aging cartilage, water content decreases and the tissue becomes stiffer (increased modulus). In early osteoarthritis, water content increases, keratan sulphate decreases, and chondroitin sulphate increases.
items.note: The biochemical differences between aging and OA are accurately represented based on the provided table in the notes.

items.q: A 10-year-old child presents with a 'snapping knee'. MRI reveals a discoid lateral meniscus. During arthroscopy, the meniscus is found to lack a posterior meniscotibial (coronary) attachment, being held only by the meniscofemoral ligament of Wrisberg. Which Watanabe type is this?
items.e: The Watanabe classification defines Type I as complete, Type II as incomplete, and Type III as the Wrisberg variant, which lacks posterior coronary attachments, making it hypermobile and prone to snapping.
items.note: The description of the Wrisberg variant and its classification as Watanabe Type III is correct.

items.q: In the structural organization of hyaline cartilage, which zone is characterized by collagen fibers oriented perpendicular to the joint surface and the highest concentration of proteoglycans?
items.e: The deep (radial) zone contains collagen fibers oriented perpendicular to the surface to resist compression, has the highest proteoglycan content, and the lowest water content.
items.note: The histological characteristics of the deep zone are correctly identified.

items.q: A 65-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset medial knee pain after a squatting maneuver. MRI shows a medial meniscus posterior root tear and a subchondral low-signal line on T2 images with surrounding marrow edema in the medial femoral condyle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Subchondral insufficiency fracture of the knee (SIFK)
items.e: Subchondral insufficiency fracture of the knee (SIFK, formerly SONK) typically occurs in elderly women and is highly associated with medial meniscus posterior root tears, which increase contact stresses leading to subchondral failure.
items.note: The clinical presentation and MRI findings perfectly match the description of SIFK in the notes.

items.q: A surgeon is performing an 'inside-out' meniscal repair for a posterior-body tear of the lateral meniscus. To avoid injury to the common peroneal nerve, where should the retractor be placed during the posterolateral approach?
o: Anterior to the lateral gastrocnemius, with biceps femoris retracted posteriorly
Between the lateral collateral ligament and the popliteus
Medial to the lateral head of the gastrocnemius
items.e: In the posterolateral approach for inside-out repair, the peroneal nerve is protected by retracting the biceps femoris posteriorly and working anterior to the lateral head of the gastrocnemius to place the spoon/retractor.
items.note: The surgical anatomy and nerve protection strategy for the posterolateral approach are correctly described.

items.q: At what degree of knee flexion does the patella typically achieve its maximum contact area with the femoral trochlea?
items.e: According to patellofemoral biomechanics, the patella contacts the trochlea at its distal pole at 20 degrees, and the contact area moves proximally and increases with flexion, reaching its maximum at approximately 90 degrees.
items.note: Correct biomechanical fact as per the reference notes.

items.q: On a true lateral radiograph, the anatomic femoral attachment of the Medial Patellofemoral Ligament (Schöttle point) is best described as being located:
o: Posterior to the extension of the posterior femoral cortex line
Just anterior to the extension of the posterior femoral cortex line
Directly on the prominence of the medial epicondyle
Distal to the origin of the medial collateral ligament
items.e: The Schöttle point is the radiographic anatomic femoral attachment of the MPFL, located between the adductor tubercle and the medial epicondyle, specifically just anterior to the posterior cortex extension line on a true lateral radiograph.
items.note: Accurate radiographic anatomy of the MPFL femoral footprint.

items.q: A 19-year-old female presents with recurrent patellar dislocations. CT imaging reveals a 'crossing sign' on the lateral view and axial images show a hypoplastic medial facet with a convex lateral facet. This morphology corresponds to which Dejour classification type?
items.e: Dejour Type C trochlear dysplasia is characterized by the crossing sign on lateral radiographs and asymmetric facets on axial views, specifically a convex lateral facet and a hypoplastic medial facet.
items.note: Correct application of the Dejour classification for trochlear dysplasia.

items.q: A 15-year-old athlete sustains a first-time non-contact knee injury with a large haemarthrosis. MRI shows a bone bruise pattern involving the medial patellar facet and the lateral femoral condyle. What is the significance of this finding?
o: It is pathognomonic for a transient lateral patellar dislocation
It indicates a high-grade ACL tear with a pivot-shift mechanism
It suggests a direct blow to the medial side of the knee
It is the characteristic pattern of a medial patellar dislocation
items.e: Bone bruises on the medial patellar facet and the lateral femoral condyle are pathognomonic for a transient lateral patellar dislocation, occurring as the patella reduces after displacing laterally.
items.note: Classic MRI finding for patellar dislocation.

items.q: During an MPFL reconstruction, if the femoral tunnel is inadvertently placed too far proximally, what is the most likely clinical complication encountered by the patient?
o: The graft will be tight in extension and loose in flexion
The graft will be tight in flexion, leading to loss of flexion and medial overload
The graft will be loose in both extension and flexion
There is an increased risk of an iatrogenic lateral patellar dislocation
items.e: Femoral tunnel malposition that is too proximal results in a graft that becomes tight as the knee flexes, which can cause loss of flexion range of motion and increased medial patellofemoral contact pressures (overload).
items.note: Important technical complication of MPFL reconstruction.

items.q: An 11-year-old boy with significant trochlear dysplasia and a lateralized tibial tubercle presents with recurrent patellar instability. Which surgical option is most appropriate to address the tendon malalignment while avoiding the risk of genu recurvatum?
items.e: In skeletally immature patients, traditional tibial tubercle osteotomies (TTO) are contraindicated due to the risk of injuring the apophysis and causing genu recurvatum. The Roux-Goldthwait procedure (transferring the lateral half of the patellar tendon medially) is a soft-tissue alternative used in these cases.
items.note: Standard management for pediatric patellar instability with open physes.

items.q: Which patellar height index is particularly useful when planning a distalisation osteotomy because the measurement is not altered by the proximal-distal position of the tibial tubercle itself?
items.e: The Caton-Deschamps index measures the distance from the inferior pole of the patellar articular surface to the anterosuperior tibial plateau. Unlike the Insall-Salvati ratio (which uses the patellar tendon length), Caton-Deschamps is not affected by a tibial tubercle osteotomy, making it the preferred index for planning and assessing distalisation.
items.note: Technical advantage of Caton-Deschamps index in surgical planning.

items.q: A 30-year-old patient presents with symptomatic inferior shoulder instability in the adducted position. Which structure is the primary static restraint to inferior translation when the arm is at the side?
o: Anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament (IGHL)
Superior glenohumeral ligament (SGHL) and coracohumeral ligament (CHL)
Posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament (IGHL)
items.e: According to the source, the SGHL and coracohumeral ligament (CHL) are the primary restraints to inferior translation in adduction (rotator interval). The anterior band of the IGHL resists anterior translation in 90 degrees of abduction and external rotation.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the specific restraints based on arm position as per standard orthopaedic anatomy and the provided notes.

items.q: A 19-year-old swimmer presents with voluntary shoulder instability. Clinical evaluation demonstrates abnormal muscle recruitment patterns during shoulder motion. According to the Stanmore triangle (Polar types), which classification and management strategy is most appropriate?
o: Polar I: Traumatic structural; Arthroscopic Bankart repair
Polar II: Atraumatic structural; Inferior capsular shift
Polar III: Muscle patterning; Biofeedback and physiotherapy
Polar III: Muscle patterning; Rotator interval closure
items.e: Polar III in the Stanmore triangle represents non-structural muscle patterning instability (abnormal muscle recruitment). The recommended management is physiotherapy and biofeedback; surgery should be avoided in these patients.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the Stanmore classification and the specific management for Polar III (muscle patterning) instability.

items.q: A 68-year-old male presents to the emergency department with an acute anterior shoulder dislocation. Following a successful closed reduction using the Kocher technique, the patient exhibits persistent weakness in shoulder abduction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: In patients over 60 years of age, the incidence of rotator cuff tears associated with shoulder dislocation is approximately 80%. Persistent weakness after reduction in an older patient is a rotator cuff tear until proved otherwise.
items.note: The question tests a critical clinical pearl regarding shoulder dislocations in the elderly, where cuff tears are far more common than recurrent instability.

items.q: During arthroscopy for recurrent anterior shoulder instability, the surgeon identifies that the anteroinferior labrum is avulsed and displaced medially and inferiorly, where it has healed to the scapular neck. This lesion, which is associated with a higher recurrence rate, is known as:
items.e: An ALPSA lesion involves the labrum being displaced medially and inferiorly on the scapular neck and healing in a malposition. It is associated with higher recurrence rates and requires mobilization before repair.
items.note: The description matches the classic definition of an ALPSA lesion, which is a common exam topic due to its higher recurrence rate if not properly mobilized.

items.q: According to the Instability Severity Index Score (ISIS), which of the following clinical or radiographic factors is assigned 2 points when calculating the risk of recurrence after arthroscopic Bankart repair?
o: Hill-Sachs lesion visible on AP radiograph in external rotation
items.e: In the ISIS score, 2 points are assigned for age under 20, competitive sport, Hill-Sachs visible on AP radiograph (external rotation), and loss of glenoid contour on AP radiograph. Contact sport and hyperlaxity are each assigned 1 point.
items.note: The question correctly tests the weighting of the ISIS score, which is a standard tool for deciding between Bankart repair and Latarjet.

items.q: The Latarjet procedure provides stability through the 'triple blocking effect' described by Patte. Which of the following is NOT a component of this effect?
o: Bony effect by extending the glenoid arc
Sling effect of the conjoint tendon on the lower subscapularis
Capsular repair to the coracoacromial ligament stump
Infraspinatus capsulotenodesis into the humeral defect
items.e: The triple blocking effect consists of the bony effect, the sling effect of the conjoint tendon (most important in abduction-ER), and the Bankart effect (capsular repair). Infraspinatus capsulotenodesis is the 'remplissage' procedure, not Latarjet.
items.note: The question correctly distinguishes the mechanisms of the Latarjet procedure from the remplissage procedure.

items.q: A 22-year-old contact athlete with recurrent instability is found to have a humeral avulsion of the glenohumeral ligament (HAGL). What is the characteristic finding on MRI for this injury?
items.e: HAGL involves avulsion of the IGHL from the humerus. On MRI, the IGHL drops down and becomes J-shaped, which is known as the 'J sign'. If missed, it leads to recurrent instability.
items.note: The question tests the specific radiographic sign associated with HAGL, which is a frequently tested 'missed' cause of instability.

items.q: According to the Warwick Agreement, which combination establishes femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) syndrome?
o: Cam or pincer morphology on imaging alone
Hip or groin symptoms, clinical signs of impingement, and cam or pincer morphology on imaging
A labral tear on MRI and restricted hip flexion
Groin pain and a positive FADIR test, irrespective of imaging
items.e: FAI syndrome requires the combination of symptoms, clinical signs and imaging findings. Cam or pincer morphology alone is common in asymptomatic people and does not establish the syndrome.
items.note: Accurately tests the Warwick Agreement triad with one clear answer.

items.q: A young athlete has a cam deformity with anterosuperior chondrolabral separation and delamination of the acetabular cartilage. Which description best fits this damage pattern?
o: Labral crushing followed by a posteroinferior contrecoup lesion
Outside-in abrasion with a carpet lesion or wave sign
Isolated posterior labral degeneration from linear contact
Primary ligamentum teres rupture from acetabular over-coverage
items.e: Cam impingement produces outside-in abrasion, often with chondrolabral separation and anterosuperior cartilage delamination—the carpet lesion or wave sign. Pincer impingement more typically crushes the labrum first and may produce a posteroinferior contrecoup lesion.
items.note: The cam damage pattern is correctly described and distinguished from pincer damage.

items.q: A patient with suspected anterior FAI has a positive FADIR test. Which statement best describes this test?
o: It is highly specific but has low sensitivity
It assesses posterior impingement during extension and external rotation
It is highly sensitive but has low specificity
It confirms an intra-articular source only when pain is relieved by the test
items.e: FADIR—flexion, adduction and internal rotation—is the anterior impingement test and is highly sensitive but poorly specific. Pain relief after a diagnostic intra-articular anaesthetic injection, rather than a positive FADIR alone, supports an intra-articular source.
items.note: Correctly tests FADIR’s sensitivity and specificity; the other options misstate its role or describe another assessment.

items.q: Which radiographic view is used to assess the alpha angle and femoral head–neck offset in suspected cam morphology?
items.e: The 45-degree Dunn view, as well as frog-leg lateral or cross-table lateral views, can assess the alpha angle and head–neck offset. The AP pelvis is used for measures such as the crossover sign and lateral centre-edge angle.
items.note: The Dunn view is the only listed view used for these cam measurements.

items.q: A 24-year-old with groin pain has a lateral centre-edge angle of 18 degrees. Which management principle is most appropriate?
o: Isolated arthroscopic labral debridement and capsulotomy
items.e: An LCEA under 20 degrees indicates dysplasia, for which periacetabular osteotomy is the stated treatment. Isolated arthroscopic labral debridement or capsulotomy in dysplasia can cause severe instability.
items.note: The LCEA indicates dysplasia, making PAO the appropriate principle; isolated arthroscopic treatment risks instability.

items.q: In which phase of throwing does elbow valgus load reach its peak?
items.e: Elbow valgus load peaks in late cocking and early acceleration, reaching about 64 Nm. The UCL's ultimate tensile strength is about 32–34 Nm, with the remainder of the load resisted by other structures, including the flexor-pronator mass.
items.note: Accurate and unambiguous.

items.q: A throwing athlete has medial elbow pain, and MR arthrography shows contrast tracking distally along the ulna from the undersurface of the UCL attachment at the sublime tubercle. This finding is known as:
items.e: The T sign describes an undersurface partial UCL tear at the sublime tubercle, with contrast tracking distally along the ulna.
items.note: The imaging finding and answer are correctly matched.

items.q: A pitcher has posterior elbow pain at ball release and loss of terminal extension. Arthroscopy is planned for a posteromedial olecranon osteophyte. Which approach best limits the risk of increasing valgus strain?
o: Resect the osteophyte and a broad segment of normal olecranon
Excise only the osteophyte and assess the UCL
Excise the olecranon tip without assessing the UCL
Treat the osteophyte with UCL reconstruction in every case
items.e: Posteromedial osteophytes can be excised arthroscopically, but resection should be limited to the osteophyte because excessive removal of normal olecranon increases UCL strain. The UCL should also be assessed because insufficiency may coexist.
items.note: Correct management principle with one defensible answer.

items.q: Which feature best distinguishes Panner disease from capitellar osteochondritis dissecans in a young athlete?
o: Panner disease is a focal anterolateral subchondral lesion in adolescents
Panner disease involves fragmentation of the whole capitellar ossific nucleus and is usually self-limiting
Panner disease commonly requires osteochondral autograft for large lesions
Panner disease is defined by an unstable fragment with loose bodies
items.e: Panner disease is an osteochondrosis involving fragmentation of the whole capitellar ossific nucleus, usually in children under 10, and typically reossifies. Capitellar OCD is a focal lesion seen more often in adolescents and has a more variable course.
items.note: Correctly distinguishes Panner disease from capitellar OCD.

items.q: A young thrower has a proximal UCL avulsion with good tissue quality. Which treatment is specifically suited to this pattern and can allow a faster return to play than reconstruction?
o: UCL repair with suture tape augmentation
UCL reconstruction using a tendon graft
Rest from throwing alone for 6–12 weeks
items.e: UCL repair with an internal brace is an option for proximal or distal avulsions with good tissue quality in young athletes. Reported return to play is about 6–7 months.
items.note: The stem specifies the tissue and tear pattern suited to repair.

items.q: A skeletally immature pitcher has medial elbow pain with widening and fragmentation of the medial epicondyle apophysis. What is the appropriate initial management?
o: Rest from throwing for about 4–6 weeks, followed by gradual return with pitch-count limits
UCL reconstruction with a tendon graft
items.e: This presentation is medial epicondyle apophysitis, or Little League elbow. Initial care is rest from throwing, followed by a gradual return with pitch-count limits.
items.note: The presentation and initial management are correctly matched.

items.q: Which is the commonest complication after UCL reconstruction?
items.e: Ulnar nerve neuritis is the commonest complication listed after UCL reconstruction. Other complications include stiffness, graft failure, medial epicondyle fracture, and medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve injury.
items.note: The complication claim is supported by the reference notes and standard descriptions.

items.q: A 24-year-old sprinter develops posterior thigh pain while accelerating. MRI shows an injury centred at the musculotendinous junction of the biceps femoris long head, with a small intratendinous component. Which BAMIC feature most strongly predicts a longer return to play and greater recurrence risk?
items.e: In BAMIC, the c subtype denotes intratendinous injury and is associated with longer return to play and higher recurrence. The classification also records injury grade from 0 to 4.
items.note: Accurately tests the prognostic significance of the BAMIC intratendinous subtype.

items.q: A footballer has a complete proximal avulsion of two hamstring tendons with 2.5 cm of retraction. He is active and presents three weeks after injury. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Eccentric strengthening alone, with surgery only if symptoms persist beyond six months
Immediate excision of the avulsed tendon ends
items.e: In an active patient, complete avulsion of two tendons with more than 2 cm of retraction is an indication for surgical repair. Early repair, generally within about 4–6 weeks, is associated with better outcomes; the sciatic nerve is nearby.
items.note: The stated tendon number, retraction and timing support early repair.

items.q: A runner presents 48 hours after an unfamiliar high-volume downhill workout with diffuse muscle soreness and a mildly raised creatine kinase. There is no marked weakness, dark urine or evidence of acute kidney injury. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?
items.e: DOMS typically develops 24–72 hours after unaccustomed eccentric exercise and may cause a mild CK elevation. Marked CK elevation and features such as myoglobinuria or acute kidney injury would raise concern for exertional rhabdomyolysis.
items.note: The original unspecified CK elevation leaves overlap with rhabdomyolysis; specifying a mild elevation and no systemic features makes the best answer clearer.

items.q: A competitive runner has focal pain over the central third of the navicular. Initial radiographs are normal, and a bone stress injury is suspected. Which imaging study is most appropriate to define this lesion?
items.e: CT is specifically useful for a navicular stress injury, particularly in its central third. This is a high-risk site because of avascularity; MRI is generally the most sensitive and specific imaging modality for bone stress injuries overall.
items.note: Appropriately distinguishes navicular-focused CT from MRI's general role in bone stress injury imaging.

items.q: A young distance runner reports predictable anterior leg pain during exercise that settles with rest, sometimes accompanied by foot numbness. Which post-exercise pressure reading meets the Pedowitz criteria for chronic exertional compartment syndrome?
items.e: Pedowitz criteria include a pressure of at least 15 mmHg before exercise, at least 30 mmHg one minute after exercise, or at least 20 mmHg five minutes after exercise. The anterior compartment is the most commonly involved.
items.note: The thresholds are stated correctly and only option D meets them.

items.q: A 6-week-old infant has a hip that can be displaced posteriorly with adduction and gentle pressure on the flexed hip. Which examination manoeuvre is being described?
items.e: The Barlow test assesses whether a hip is dislocatable, using adduction and posterior pressure on the flexed hip. Ortolani reduces a dislocated hip with abduction and elevation of the greater trochanter.
items.note: Correctly describes the Barlow manoeuvre and distinguishes it from reduction testing.

items.q: In an infant older than 3 months, which clinical finding is the most reliable sign of DDH?
o: Positive Galeazzi sign in bilateral DDH
items.e: Limited abduction, particularly under 60 degrees in flexion or when asymmetric, is the most reliable sign in an older infant. Skin-fold asymmetry is unreliable, and Galeazzi sign is negative in bilateral DDH.
items.note: The age-specific examination finding and the distractor descriptions are accurate.

items.q: Which presentation is the strongest single risk factor for developmental dysplasia of the hip?
items.e: Frank breech presentation, with the hips flexed and knees extended, is the strongest single risk factor listed. Female sex, first-born status and oligohydramnios are also associated with DDH.
items.note: Frank breech is correctly identified as the strongest single risk factor.

items.q: A 2-month-old has a stable hip with a Graf alpha angle of 55 degrees and a beta angle of 65 degrees. What is the appropriate management?
o: Repeat ultrasound in 6 weeks to 3 months
items.e: An alpha angle of 50–59 degrees in an infant under 3 months is Graf type IIa, representing physiological immaturity. Repeat ultrasound at 6 weeks to 3 months is recommended.
items.note: The measurements and age fit Graf type IIa, for which follow-up ultrasound is appropriate.

items.q: On an AP radiograph of an infant's pelvis, where should the femoral head ossific nucleus lie in a normally located hip, using Hilgenreiner and Perkin lines?
items.e: The femoral head ossific nucleus, or medial metaphyseal beak, should lie in the inferomedial quadrant. The quadrant is defined by Hilgenreiner's horizontal line and Perkin's vertical line.
items.note: The quadrant and the lines used to define it are correctly stated.

items.q: An infant treated in a Pavlik harness develops quadriceps weakness. The hips had been held in more than 120 degrees of flexion. What is the most likely complication?
items.e: Excessive hip flexion in a Pavlik harness can cause femoral nerve palsy, often presenting with quadriceps weakness; the harness should be stopped or adjusted. Excessive abduction is associated with AVN.
items.note: The position and clinical deficit correctly identify femoral nerve palsy.

items.q: Which feature best distinguishes teratologic hip dislocation from the usual spectrum of DDH?
o: It is typically reducible with an Ortolani manoeuvre
It occurs in utero and is irreducible
It presents only after the femoral head ossific nucleus appears
It is defined by an alpha angle of 50–59 degrees
items.e: Teratologic dislocation occurs in utero and is irreducible, often in association with neuromuscular syndromes such as arthrogryposis or myelomeningocele. It has a worse prognosis and is managed with early open reduction.
items.note: The defining distinction is accurately stated; the associated syndrome examples and management in the explanation are also consistent.

items.q: A 6-year-old has a limp and restricted hip abduction, and early Perthes disease is suspected. Which investigation best defines the extent of femoral-head involvement before radiographic changes are apparent?
items.e: MRI can detect early Perthes disease and define the extent of epiphyseal involvement before radiographic changes appear. Bone scan can demonstrate avascularity early, but the stem asks about defining the extent of involvement.
items.note: As written, bone scan and MRI are both supported for early detection; specifying extent makes MRI the single best answer.

items.q: An 8-year-old with Perthes disease is assessed at the start of fragmentation. The lateral pillar retains just over 50% of its original height. Which Herring group applies?
items.e: Herring group B retains more than 50% of the lateral pillar height. Group B/C border includes a pillar at about 50% or one that is narrow or poorly ossified.
items.note: The threshold and assessment timing are stated clearly, giving one answer.

items.q: Which Waldenström stage of Perthes disease is the period of greatest mechanical vulnerability to femoral-head deformation?
items.e: During fragmentation, resorption weakens the epiphysis, making it especially vulnerable to deformation. Containment is aimed at protecting the head during this stage.
items.note: The tested stage and its defining mechanical risk are unambiguous.

items.q: At skeletal maturity, a patient with previous Perthes disease has a flat femoral head and a normal-shaped acetabulum. Which Stulberg class and osteoarthritis risk best fit this outcome?
o: Class III; mild-to-moderate risk in later adulthood
Class IV; moderate risk in middle age
items.e: Stulberg class V describes a flat head with a normal acetabulum, producing aspherical incongruency and a risk of severe early osteoarthritis. A flat head with a flat acetabulum is class IV.
items.note: The morphology distinguishes class V from class IV and supports a single answer.

items.q: On an AP pelvic radiograph of an adolescent with suspected SCFE, Klein’s line, drawn along the superior femoral neck, fails to intersect the lateral epiphysis. What is this radiographic sign called?
items.e: Failure of Klein’s line to intersect the lateral epiphysis is the Trethowan sign and supports SCFE. Shenton sign concerns disruption of the smooth arc of the hip, while the crescent and Gage signs are associated with Perthes disease.
items.note: Klein line and Trethowan sign are closely related terms, so the original options offered two defensible answers.

items.q: Which classification distinguishes stable from unstable slipped capital femoral epiphysis according to the patient’s ability to bear weight?
items.e: The Loder classification is based on weight-bearing ability: a stable slip allows the patient to walk, with or without crutches, whereas an unstable slip does not.
items.note: The classification and defining criterion are stated accurately.

items.q: Which radiographic method is used to quantify the severity of a slipped capital femoral epiphysis by comparing the epiphyseal-shaft angle with the opposite hip?
items.e: The Southwick angle is used to assess the degree of slip, conventionally by comparing the affected hip with the contralateral side. The other listed systems classify Perthes disease.
items.note: The method and comparison are correctly described and the alternatives are distinct.

items.q: In the Pirani scoring system for congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV), which of the following physical signs is a component of the Midfoot Contracture Score (MFCS)?
items.e: The Pirani Midfoot Contracture Score (MFCS, max 3) consists of the curved lateral border, medial crease, and lateral head of talus coverage. Empty heel, posterior crease, and rigid equinus constitute the Hindfoot Contracture Score (HFCS, max 3).
items.note: Accurate, classic Pirani scoring question directly supported by Campbell's and exam notes.

items.q: In patients with congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV), which vascular abnormality is most commonly present, necessitating caution to preserve the remaining dominant vessel during surgical release?
o: Hypoplasia or absence of the anterior tibial artery
Complete aplasia of the peroneal artery
Obliteration of the posterior tibial artery
Duplication of the medial plantar artery
