items.e: The anterior tibial artery is hypoplastic or absent in up to 85% of CTEV cases (dorsalis pedis is frequently absent). Therefore, extreme care must be taken during posteromedial surgery to avoid damaging the posterior tibial artery, which is often the sole arterial supply to the foot.
items.note: Standard high-yield anatomical pearl in paediatric orthopaedics and surgical CTEV anatomy.

items.q: During serial manipulation of an idiopathic clubfoot using the Ponseti method, placing counter-pressure over the calcaneocuboid joint rather than the lateral head of the talus (Kite's error) leads to which mechanical failure?
o: It causes iatrogenic dorsal subluxation of the navicular
It locks the calcaneus, preventing its abduction and rotation beneath the talus
It causes excessive forefoot supination, precipitating an acute rocker-bottom deformity
It stretches the spring ligament, inducing severe secondary hindfoot valgus
items.e: Kite's error consists of placing counter-pressure on the calcaneocuboid joint instead of the lateral talar head. This locks the calcaneus against the talus, preventing it from abducting and rotating medially/everting beneath the talus into normal alignment.
items.note: Crucial technical biomechanical concept of the Ponseti method, verified in Campbell's.

items.q: A 3-year-old child previously treated successfully in infancy for idiopathic clubfoot presents with dynamic supination of the forefoot during gait and walks on the lateral border of the foot. On examination, the deformity is fully passively correctable, and radiographs reveal an ossified lateral cuneiform. What is the most appropriate surgical treatment?
o: Lateral column shortening via calcaneocuboid fusion (Evans procedure)
Posteromedial soft-tissue release with Achilles lengthening
Tibialis anterior tendon transfer to the lateral cuneiform
items.e: Dynamic supination during gait due to an overactive tibialis anterior is a common relapse pattern. When the foot remains passively flexible and the lateral cuneiform is ossified (typically in a child over 2.5–3 years of age), the definitive procedure is tibialis anterior tendon transfer (TATT) to the lateral (third) cuneiform.
items.note: Standard surgical indication and management for Ponseti relapse with dynamic supination.

items.q: A newborn is evaluated for a rigid rocker-bottom foot deformity with a palpable prominence on the plantar-medial aspect of the midfoot. Which radiographic finding on a forced (maximal) plantarflexion lateral view differentiates congenital vertical talus (CVT) from congenital oblique talus?
o: The calcaneal pitch angle normalises completely to zero degrees in CVT
The anterior process of the calcaneus impinges on the navicular in congenital oblique talus
The talonavicular dislocation fails to reduce in CVT, with the talar axis remaining plantar to the first metatarsal
The talocalcaneal angle decreases to less than 20 degrees in congenital oblique talus
items.e: In congenital vertical talus, the dorsal talonavicular dislocation is rigid and fails to reduce on a maximal plantarflexion lateral radiograph, leaving the longitudinal axis of the talus directed plantar to the first metatarsal. In contrast, congenital oblique talus is flexible, and the talonavicular joint reduces in maximal plantarflexion.
items.note: Pathognomonic radiographic differentiator for vertical vs oblique talus.

items.q: According to the Bleck classification for metatarsus adductus, where does the heel bisector line project in a foot with moderate deformity?
o: Between the third and fourth toes
Between the fourth and fifth toes
items.e: The Bleck classification evaluates metatarsus adductus by using the longitudinal heel bisector line: normal passes through the second-third toe web space; mild passes through the third toe; moderate passes between the third and fourth toes; and severe passes between the fourth and fifth toes.
items.note: Exact classification standard from Campbell's and paediatric orthopaedic literature.

items.q: A 12-year-old child with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease presents with bilateral cavovarus feet. On performing the Coleman block test, placing a block under the lateral border of the foot while allowing the first ray to drop results in complete correction of the hindfoot varus into valgus. What does this test finding indicate?
o: The hindfoot varus is rigid and mandates a Dwyer lateral closing-wedge osteotomy
The hindfoot varus is flexible and forefoot-driven by a plantarflexed first ray
There is an underlying rigid subtalar tarsal coalition requiring excision
The claw toes are driving hindfoot stiffness and require flexor tenotomies
items.e: The Coleman block test uncouples the forefoot from the hindfoot. Correction of the hindfoot varus when the first ray drops off the block confirms a flexible, forefoot-driven hindfoot varus (due to a plantarflexed first ray from strong peroneus longus action), which can be managed with forefoot procedures without requiring a calcaneal osteotomy.
items.note: Classic diagnostic test interpretation tested regularly in orthopaedic postgraduate exams.

items.q: An 11-year-old child presents with a rigid painful flatfoot, recurrent ankle sprains, and peroneal muscle spasm. A lateral radiograph reveals an 'anteater nose' sign (an elongated anterior process of the calcaneus). Which radiographic projection is best to confirm this specific coalition?
items.e: The 'anteater nose' sign represents elongation of the anterior calcaneal process in calcaneonavicular (CN) coalition. CN coalitions typically present between 8 and 12 years of age and are best visualised on a 45-degree internal oblique radiograph of the foot (whereas talocalcaneal coalitions are evaluated on the Harris axial view or CT).
items.note: Specific standard radiographic view for CN coalition, widely referenced in Campbell's.

items.q: A 9-month-old infant is brought to the clinic because she has stopped bearing weight on her right lower limb after a minor stumble. Plain radiographs reveal an undisplaced, faint spiral fracture of the distal tibia with intact fibula. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: A toddler's fracture is an undisplaced spiral or oblique fracture of the distal tibial shaft seen in children aged 9 months to 3 years who are beginning to walk. It typically results from a mild twisting injury, may be subtle or invisible on initial radiographs, and is usually accidental.
items.note: Fully accurate, supported by standard paediatric orthopaedic literature and the reference notes.

items.q: A 6-year-old child with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy (GMFCS level IV) is monitored under a hip surveillance protocol. The latest AP pelvis radiograph demonstrates a Reimer migration percentage (MP) of 44% in the right hip with significant acetabular dysplasia. The hip is painless, and hip abduction in extension is 25 degrees. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Isolated percutaneous adductor and psoas tenotomies
Reconstructive surgery with varus derotation osteotomy and pelvic osteotomy
Proximal femoral resection interposition arthroplasty (Castle procedure)
items.e: A Reimer migration percentage exceeding 40% with acetabular dysplasia in a child over 4–5 years represents progressive hip subluxation where isolated soft-tissue releases carry high failure rates. Comprehensive reconstructive surgery (varus derotational femoral osteotomy combined with a pelvic osteotomy such as Dega or San Diego) is the gold standard before dislocation becomes irreducible or the femoral head becomes severely deformed.
items.note: Accurate, guideline-concordant question on cerebral palsy hip surveillance and reconstruction thresholds.

items.q: A 10-year-old boy with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy (GMFCS III) develops progressive crouch gait with excessive stance-phase knee flexion and increased ankle dorsiflexion. Review of his surgical history reveals a prior bilateral procedure performed at age 5 for equinus gait. Which iatrogenic complication is the most common cause of this deterioration?
o: Over-lengthening of the Achilles tendon disrupting the plantarflexor–knee extension couple
Over-release of the distal hamstring tendons causing genu recurvatum
Distal transfer of the rectus femoris to the gracilis tendon
Intramuscular lengthening of the psoas tendon over the pelvic brim
items.e: Over-lengthening of the Achilles tendon or gastrocnemius-soleus complex causes triceps surae insufficiency, which compromises the plantarflexor–knee extension couple. In stance, the ground reaction force falls behind the knee axis, leading to uncontrolled ankle dorsiflexion, excessive knee flexion, and an energy-consuming progressive crouch gait.
items.note: Classic and high-yield concept tested frequently in paediatric orthopaedic superspeciality exams.

items.q: A 4-year-old girl with a lumbar hypertrichosis tuft undergoes spinal MRI for progressive in-toeing and asymmetrical calf wasting. Imaging demonstrates a split cord malformation. According to Pang's classification, which pathological feature definitively differentiates a Type I from a Type II split cord malformation?
o: Type I has two hemicords sharing a single dural tube with an intradural non-rigid fibrous septum
Type I has two hemicords housed within separate dural tubes separated by a rigid osteocartilaginous spur
Type I features an open placode with continuous CSF leakage, whereas Type II is covered by intact skin
Type I possesses a dilated central canal (hydromyelia), whereas Type II cord tissue is completely normal
items.e: Pang Type I split cord malformation is characterized by two hemicords, each enclosed within its own individual dural sleeve, separated by a rigid osseous or osteocartilaginous median spur. Pang Type II consists of two hemicords residing within a single common dural sac, separated only by a non-rigid fibrous median septum.
items.note: Accurate anatomical definition of Pang's classification of split cord malformations.

items.q: A 14-year-old boy with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease presents with a symptomatic cavovarus deformity of the right foot. On physical examination, performing the Coleman block test results in full correction of the hindfoot varus into valgus when the first metatarsal is allowed to drop off the block. Which surgical intervention is the primary directed treatment for this deformity?
o: Plantar fascia release and first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy
Triple arthrodesis with medial soft-tissue release
Tendon transfer of the tibialis posterior to the dorsum alone
items.e: When the hindfoot varus corrects fully on the Coleman block test, it confirms a flexible hindfoot deformity driven primarily by forefoot pronation (a plantarflexed first ray pulled down by an overactive peroneus longus). Management focuses on correcting the primary driver via plantar fascia release and a dorsiflexion osteotomy of the first metatarsal, avoiding an unnecessary calcaneal osteotomy.
items.note: Classic application of the Coleman block test in neuromuscular cavovarus foot reconstruction.

items.q: In children with spastic cerebral palsy presenting with a stiff-knee gait during the swing phase, which physical examination test specifically assesses spasticity of the responsible muscle, and which surgical procedure is standardly performed?
o: Thomas test; psoas lengthening over the brim
Duncan-Ely test; distal rectus femoris transfer to semitendinosus or gracilis
Staheli prone test; proximal hamstring release
items.e: Stiff-knee gait in cerebral palsy is characterized by decreased and delayed peak knee flexion in the swing phase, driven by inappropriate swing-phase spasticity of the rectus femoris. The Duncan-Ely test (rapid prone knee flexion eliciting spontaneous hip flexion) detects rectus spasticity, and distal rectus femoris transfer (Perry procedure) to the semitendinosus or gracilis converts it from an extensor into a knee flexor.
items.note: Standard gait pathology concept in spastic CP.

items.q: A child with myelomeningocele is assessed for functional motor level. Physical examination reveals active hip flexion (grade 4/5), active hip adduction (grade 4/5), and active knee extension (grade 4/5). There is no active knee flexion, ankle dorsiflexion, or ankle plantarflexion. What is the Hoffer/Sharrard motor level and expected long-term ambulatory prognosis?
o: L2 motor level; non-ambulatory, dependent on wheelchair for mobility
L3 motor level; household or limited community ambulation with KAFOs or AFOs
L4 motor level; independent community ambulation with ground-reaction AFOs
L5 motor level; independent community ambulation without any orthotic support
items.e: An intact quadriceps (knee extension) alongside iliopsoas (hip flexion) and adductors defines an L3 motor level (L4 requires tibialis anterior/dorsiflexion). Children with an L3 neurological level typically achieve household or limited community ambulation during childhood using knee-ankle-foot orthoses (KAFOs) or ankle-foot orthoses (AFOs) with crutches, though many transition to wheelchairs for distance in adulthood.
items.note: Standard Hoffer/Sharrard classification and ambulatory functional prognosis for myelomeningocele.

items.q: In an adolescent with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy (GMFCS V) who has an intractable, chronically dislocated, painful hip with severe femoral head erosion, which procedure comprises femoral head-and-neck excision combined with a subtrochanteric valgus-producing osteotomy?
items.e: The McHale procedure combines femoral head and neck excision with a subtrochanteric valgus osteotomy and soft-tissue interposition. The valgus osteotomy directs the lesser trochanter towards the acetabulum, preventing proximal femoral migration, reducing painful pelvic impingement, and facilitating stable perineal hygiene and seating in non-ambulant patients.
items.note: Accurate distinction between salvage procedures for painful neuromuscular dislocated hips.

items.q: A 12-year-old child with spastic hemiplegic cerebral palsy presents with wrist flexion and ulnar deviation contracture with poor active wrist extension. Voluntary active finger extension is demonstrable when the wrist is passively supported in neutral. Which surgical transfer is the classic Green transfer utilized for this presentation?
o: Transfer of flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) to extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB)
Transfer of flexor carpi radialis (FCR) to extensor digitorum communis (EDC)
Transfer of pronator teres (PT) to supinator
Transfer of brachioradialis (BR) to extensor pollicis longus (EPL)
items.e: The classic Green procedure is the transfer of the flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) tendon into the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB). This eliminates the deforming wrist flexion-ulnar deviation force of the spastic FCU and repurposes it to provide active, balanced wrist extension, facilitating effective finger grasp and release.
items.note: Standard eponym and tendon transfer procedure in upper extremity cerebral palsy.

items.q: A 3-year-old child presents with a waddling gait, mild short stature, genu varum, and bilateral coxa vara. Plain radiographs show widening, flaring, and irregularity of the long bone metaphyses, mimicking nutritional rickets. However, serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels are completely normal. Which gene is mutated in this condition?
items.e: Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia is an autosomal dominant condition caused by mutations in COL10A1 (type X collagen). It presents with mild short stature, coxa vara, and rickets-like metaphyseal flaring, but with strictly normal serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and vitamin D levels.
items.note: Accurate, high-yield skeletal dysplasia question with unambiguous findings directly supported by the syllabus.

items.q: A child presents with recurrent fractures, moderate limb deformity, and normal white sclerae. Radiographs demonstrate calcification of the interosseous membrane of the forearm with a radial head dislocation, alongside exuberant hyperplastic callus formation following a healed diaphyseal fracture. Which type of osteogenesis imperfecta does this patient have?
items.e: Osteogenesis imperfecta type V is characterized by normal (white) sclerae, hyperplastic callus formation, radial head dislocation, and calcification of the forearm interosseous membrane (restricting pronation and supination), caused by mutations in IFITM5.
items.note: Directly tests classic distinguishing hallmarks of type V osteogenesis imperfecta.

items.q: An infant with clinically confirmed achondroplasia presents with progressive generalized hypotonia and episodic central apnoea during sleep. What is the most critical anatomical abnormality responsible for this presentation?
items.e: In infants with achondroplasia, foramen magnum stenosis can cause cervicomedullary compression manifesting as hypotonia, central apnoea, and an increased risk of sudden death. It requires urgent screening with MRI/polysomnography and may necessitate suboccipital decompression.
items.note: Standard, critical clinical knowledge point for paediatric orthopaedics and exam preparation.

items.q: A newborn is evaluated for skeletal dysplasia. Physical examination reveals a proximally placed, abducted first metacarpal ('hitchhiker thumb'), bilateral cystic swellings of the pinnae ('cauliflower ears'), cleft palate, and severe, rigid clubfeet resistant to conservative casting. What is the causative gene for this condition?
items.e: Diastrophic dysplasia is an autosomal recessive dysplasia caused by mutations in the SLC26A2 sulfate transporter gene. Classical features include the 'hitchhiker thumb', cystic ear swelling in infancy ('cauliflower ear'), rigid clubfeet, and progressive cervical kyphosis.
items.note: Spotless question evaluating pathognomonic phenotypic signs matched to gene mutation.

items.q: Paediatric patients with certain skeletal dysplasias require a routine upper cervical spine instability screen (flexion-extension radiographs with or without MRI) prior to general anaesthesia. In which of the following conditions is atlantoaxial instability due to odontoid hypoplasia a well-recognized indication for this screening?
items.e: Patients with Morquio syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis IV) have odontoid hypoplasia predisposing to atlantoaxial instability and cord compression. A cervical instability screen is essential before general anaesthesia, and occipitocervical fusion is often required.
items.note: Essential clinical concept regarding pre-operative anaesthesia clearance in skeletal dysplasias.

items.q: A 7-year-old child presents with marked shoulder hypermobility and is able to appose both shoulders anteriorly across the midline of the chest. Radiographs reveal bilateral clavicular hypoplasia, delayed fontanelle closure, and numerous wormian bones. Which of the following orthopaedic abnormalities is classically associated with this condition?
o: Calcification of the forearm interosseous membrane
items.e: Cleidocranial dysplasia (caused by RUNX2 mutations) features clavicular hypoplasia/aplasia, wide fontanelles with wormian bones, supernumerary teeth, wide pubic symphysis, and coxa vara. When the Hilgenreiner-epiphyseal angle exceeds 60 degrees, valgus osteotomy is indicated.
items.note: Excellent question testing the orthopaedic lower extremity manifestations of cleidocranial dysplasia.

items.q: A 6-year-old child presents with bilateral hip pain and a waddling gait. Radiographs show irregular, flattened capital femoral epiphyses bilaterally. Which radiographic finding most reliably distinguishes Multiple Epiphyseal Dysplasia (MED) from bilateral Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease?
o: Bilateral, symmetrical epiphyseal changes at the same radiographic stage
Asynchronous involvement with femoral heads in different stages of fragmentation
items.e: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED) characteristically presents with bilateral, symmetrical femoral head epiphyseal changes that are at the exact same stage of involvement. In contrast, bilateral Perthes disease is typically asynchronous and presents at differing radiographic stages in each hip.
items.note: Core differentiator between MED and Perthes disease repeatedly tested in orthopaedic superspeciality exams.

items.q: A short-statured patient is evaluated for recurrent low-energy fractures. Radiographs reveal generalized osteosclerosis (dense bones), persistent open cranial fontanelles, an obtuse mandibular angle, and distinct acro-osteolysis of the terminal phalanges. This disorder is caused by an inherited deficiency of which protein?
items.e: Pyknodysostosis is an autosomal recessive osteosclerotic dysplasia caused by mutations in the cathepsin K gene. Key features include generalized dense bones, short stature, acro-osteolysis of the terminal phalanges, open cranial fontanelles, an obtuse mandibular angle, and repeated fractures.
items.note: Clinically and genetically accurate question differentiating osteosclerotic disorders.

items.q: A 10-month-old infant develops acute haematogenous osteomyelitis of the proximal femur. Which anatomical feature best explains the risk of infection extending across the physis into the epiphysis and hip joint?
o: The physis is normally a barrier to infection throughout infancy
Transphyseal vessels cross the physis at this age
The periosteum is firmly attached to the metaphysis
Metaphyseal vessels drain directly into the joint in all children
items.e: In children under about 18 months, transphyseal vessels allow infection to cross from the metaphysis into the epiphysis; at the proximal femur, this can also involve the hip joint. The physis is generally a barrier in older children, and direct metaphyseal-joint communication does not occur in all children.
items.note: The original proximal tibia stem did not reliably support extension into the joint; the proximal femur is a recognised site where metaphyseal infection can reach the hip.

items.q: During the evolution of acute haematogenous osteomyelitis, pus escapes through openings in the involucrum. These openings are called:
items.e: Cloacae are openings in the involucrum through which pus escapes. A sequestrum is devitalised bone, while the involucrum is new bone laid down by the elevated periosteum.
items.note: Correct terminology and a clear single best answer.

items.q: A 2-year-old has a mild limp following a recent upper respiratory infection. The child is afebrile, and inflammatory markers are normal or only mildly raised. Joint fluid is being investigated for a suspected osteoarticular infection. Which approach best improves detection of the likely organism?
o: Inoculate the fluid into blood-culture bottles and use PCR
Request routine culture only, because the organism grows readily on standard media
Request fungal culture as the primary test
Use Gram stain alone to exclude infection if negative
items.e: Kingella kingae commonly causes osteoarticular infection in young children and can present with mild illness and little fever. It grows poorly on standard media, so blood-culture bottle inoculation and PCR improve detection.
items.note: The age, mild presentation and detection strategy fit Kingella kingae.

items.q: Which laboratory marker is most useful for monitoring response to effective treatment of acute haematogenous osteomyelitis?
o: ESR, because it usually normalises within about a week
WBC count, because it has a defined peak at 48 hours
CRP, because it generally normalises within about a week
Blood culture, because it is positive in nearly all cases
items.e: CRP rises within 6–8 hours, peaks at about 48 hours and generally normalises within about a week of effective treatment. ESR rises over days and may remain elevated for weeks.
items.note: CRP is the best response marker among the options; the other stated reasons are inaccurate.

items.q: A child has persistent focal bone pain and fever, with concern for osteomyelitis and a possible adjacent abscess. Which imaging investigation is the choice for defining marrow involvement and the extent of infection?
items.e: MRI is the investigation of choice for osteomyelitis and can show marrow oedema, abscesses, physeal involvement and adjacent joint or muscle infection. Contrast can help define abscesses.
items.note: MRI is correctly identified for assessing marrow and the extent of infection.

items.q: A laceration extends from the A1 pulley to the FDS insertion, leaving both FDS and FDP within the flexor sheath. Which Verdan zone is involved?
items.e: Zone II extends from the A1 pulley to the FDS insertion and contains both flexor tendons within the tight fibro-osseous sheath. It is traditionally called the “no man’s land.”
items.note: Accurate definition and classic description of zone II; single best answer.

items.q: A ring-finger FDP avulsion has retracted into the palm, with both vincula ruptured. Which Leddy–Packer type is this, and what is the recommended repair window?
o: Type IV; fix the fragment and tendon
items.e: Type I injuries retract into the palm after rupture of both vincula. Repair is recommended within 7–10 days because of poor vascularity and rapid myostatic contracture.
items.note: Classification and timing match the reference notes.

items.q: Which statement about flexor tendon repair is correct?
o: Strength is independent of the number of core strands crossing the repair
A gap exceeding 3 mm increases rupture and adhesion risk
Core purchase should be about 2–3 mm from the cut end
items.e: A repair gap greater than 3 mm is associated with increased rupture and adhesion risk. Repair strength increases with the number of core strands crossing the repair, while an epitendinous suture adds strength and reduces gliding resistance.
items.note: The keyed statement and the contrasts with the other options are supported by standard repair principles.

items.q: Which flexor pulley is considered the most important biomechanically in the thumb?
items.e: The thumb has A1, oblique and A2 pulleys. The oblique pulley is the most important biomechanically.
items.note: The thumb pulley anatomy and relative importance are stated in the reference notes.

items.q: A patient develops delayed loss of thumb interphalangeal extension several weeks after an undisplaced distal radius fracture. Which tendon and dorsal wrist compartment are classically implicated?
items.e: The EPL passes through the third dorsal wrist compartment, ulnar to Lister’s tubercle. Attrition rupture can occur 4–8 weeks after an undisplaced distal radius fracture.
items.note: Classic tendon, compartment, and delayed complication are correctly matched.

items.q: A proximal laceration of an EDC tendon is explored, but the injured finger can still extend. Which structure can account for this finding?
items.e: Juncturae tendinum connect the EDC tendons on the dorsum of the hand and can mask a proximal EDC laceration by allowing extension to persist.
items.note: Juncturae tendinum are the standard explanation for masked proximal EDC lacerations.

items.q: Following flexor tendon reconstruction, a patient shows paradoxical PIPJ extension when attempting finger flexion. Which complication best describes this finding?
items.e: Lumbrical-plus finger causes paradoxical PIPJ extension on attempted flexion. It can result when the FDP is cut distal to the lumbrical origin or when a graft is too long.
items.note: The defining clinical finding and relevant causes match lumbrical-plus finger.

items.q: After a closed nerve injury, a patient has a local conduction block but the axon remains intact. There is no advancing Tinel sign, and complete recovery is expected within days to about 12 weeks. How is this injury classified?
items.e: Neurapraxia is a local conduction block with an intact axon and corresponds to Sunderland grade I. Recovery is complete, and there is no advancing Tinel sign.
items.note: Accurate classification and recovery features; one clear answer.

items.q: A patient with carpal tunnel syndrome reports nocturnal tingling in the radial three and a half digits but has normal sensation over the palm. Which anatomical feature best explains the spared palm?
o: The palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum
The recurrent motor branch supplies sensation to the palm
The median nerve gives off its digital branches proximal to the wrist
The flexor retinaculum forms the floor of the carpal tunnel
items.e: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the wrist and passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum. It therefore escapes compression within the carpal tunnel.
items.note: Anatomically accurate explanation of palmar sparing.

items.q: Following a distal radius fracture, a patient develops progressively worsening median nerve symptoms at the wrist. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Night splinting in neutral and review in several weeks
Corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel
Nerve conduction studies before deciding on treatment
items.e: Progressive acute carpal tunnel syndrome after a distal radius fracture warrants urgent release. Waiting for electrodiagnostic testing or trying routine non-operative treatment risks ongoing compression.
items.note: Progressive acute CTS after distal radius fracture warrants urgent decompression.

items.q: In a suspected brachial plexus injury, the patient has numb skin but sensory nerve action potentials are preserved. Which lesion does this finding indicate?
o: Median nerve compression at the carpal tunnel
Axonal injury distal to the dorsal root ganglion
items.e: Preserved SNAPs despite sensory loss point to a preganglionic lesion, such as root avulsion. The dorsal root ganglion cell body remains intact, so the distal sensory response is preserved.
items.note: Classic electrodiagnostic distinction between preganglionic and postganglionic lesions.

items.q: After a nerve injury, when should NCS and EMG generally be performed to allow denervation changes to become apparent?
items.e: NCS and EMG are generally deferred for about 3 weeks because Wallerian degeneration must occur before denervation changes appear. Fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves indicate denervation.
items.note: The timing is appropriate for detecting denervation changes.

items.q: A patient with a traction injury has anaesthesia in the hand, but sensory nerve action potentials from the affected limb remain preserved. Which lesion best explains this finding?
o: Preganglionic root avulsion proximal to the dorsal root ganglion
Postganglionic plexus rupture distal to the dorsal root ganglion
Isolated injury to a terminal nerve
items.e: In a preganglionic avulsion, the dorsal root ganglion cell bodies and peripheral sensory axons remain intact, so SNAPs are preserved despite sensory loss. Postganglionic lesions generally abolish the SNAP.
items.note: Clear single-best answer testing a standard distinction between preganglionic and postganglionic injury.

items.q: After a shoulder dislocation, a patient has weakness of shoulder abduction and elbow flexion. The injury is localized to the cords and terminal branches beneath pectoralis minor. What is the expected general prognosis compared with a root avulsion?
o: Worse, because infraclavicular injuries are usually preganglionic
Better, because infraclavicular injuries are usually postganglionic
Identical, because injury level does not affect recovery potential
Worse, because postganglionic injuries have no potential for repair
items.e: Infraclavicular injuries involving cords or branches are generally postganglionic and have a better prognosis than root avulsions. Postganglionic lesions may recover spontaneously or be treated with repair or grafting.
items.note: The stated infraclavicular location supports a postganglionic lesion and the prognosis comparison is clear.

items.q: Which statement about the divisions of the brachial plexus is correct?
o: They lie between the anterior and middle scalene muscles and give the long thoracic nerve
They lie in the posterior triangle and give the suprascapular nerve
They lie behind the clavicle and have no branches
They are named by their relation to the second part of the axillary artery
items.e: The anterior and posterior divisions lie behind the clavicle and give no branches. The cords, rather than the divisions, are named by their relation to the second part of the axillary artery.
items.note: Accurate anatomy question with one unambiguous correct option.

items.q: A patient with a closed traction injury has no Horner syndrome or other strong evidence of root avulsion. The lesion is thought likely to be postganglionic. In the absence of vascular injury, what is the usual initial plan?
o: Observe for about 3 months, then explore if there is no clinical or EMG recovery
Defer assessment until 12–18 months have elapsed
items.e: For a closed injury likely to be postganglionic, observation for about 3 months is usual, followed by exploration if recovery is absent. Results deteriorate after about 6 months, with motor end-plate degeneration by 12–18 months.
items.note: The stipulated likely postganglionic lesion and absence of an urgent associated injury support the stated observation period.

items.q: During reconstruction of a flail shoulder, the operative plan is to transfer the distal spinal accessory nerve to the suprascapular nerve. Which additional shoulder nerve transfer is described for restoring shoulder function?
o: Ulnar fascicle to the biceps motor branch
Median fascicle to the brachialis motor branch
Triceps long-head branch of the radial nerve to the axillary nerve
Thoracodorsal nerve to the musculocutaneous nerve
items.e: The triceps long-head branch of the radial nerve can be transferred to the axillary nerve to restore shoulder function. The ulnar and median fascicle transfers listed are used to restore elbow flexion.
items.note: The described axillary nerve transfer is a shoulder reconstruction option; the fascicular distractors target elbow flexion.

items.q: In a pan-plexus injury requiring nerve transfers, which functional goal is generally prioritized first?
items.e: The stated priority is elbow flexion first, followed by shoulder stability or abduction, hand sensation, and then wrist and finger function.
items.note: The priority sequence is explicitly supported and the options are distinct functional goals.

items.q: A patient has persistent snuffbox tenderness after a fall, but initial scaphoid-series radiographs are normal. Which investigation is the gold standard for detecting an occult scaphoid fracture?
o: CT along the scaphoid’s long axis
items.e: Up to about 20% of scaphoid fractures are occult on initial radiographs. MRI is the gold standard for occult fractures and is most useful within the first few days.
items.note: Correct answer and investigation role are supported; the options are distinguishable.

items.q: The dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery enters the scaphoid at the waist and supplies most of the bone by retrograde flow. Which fracture location therefore carries the greatest risk of avascular necrosis?
items.e: The dorsal arterial supply reaches the proximal pole by retrograde flow. A proximal-pole fracture therefore has the greatest risk of avascular necrosis and non-union.
items.note: The vascular anatomy and resulting risk ranking are supported and unambiguous.

items.q: A complete scaphoid waist fracture has a 2 mm displacement. Which treatment is most appropriate?
o: Fixation with a headless compression screw
items.e: A displaced waist fracture of this degree is unstable and is appropriately treated with fixation, commonly using a headless compression screw along the scaphoid’s central axis. Casting durations in options A and B apply to more stable fracture patterns.
items.note: The original 1.5 mm value falls within a variably stated 1–2 mm threshold; 2 mm makes the fixation indication clear.

items.q: A scaphoid fracture is classified as Herbert B3. Which description matches this type?
items.e: Herbert B3 denotes an unstable acute proximal-pole fracture. Incomplete waist fractures are A2, distal oblique fractures are B1, and fibrous non-union is D1.
items.note: The classification and distractors are accurate and clearly differentiated.

items.q: A patient with longstanding scaphoid non-union has arthritis involving the radial styloid–scaphoid and scaphocapitate joints, while the capitolunate joint is preserved. What is the SNAC stage?
items.e: SNAC stage II includes the radial styloid–scaphoid and scaphocapitate joints. Capitolunate arthritis is added in stage III.
items.note: The described pattern maps directly to the stated SNAC staging.

items.q: Which part of the scapholunate interosseous ligament is the strongest and most important stabilising component?
o: All three parts are equally strong
items.e: The dorsal part of the scapholunate interosseous ligament is its strongest and most important component. Secondary stabilisers include the dorsal intercarpal and dorsal radiocarpal ligaments.
items.note: The tested ligament anatomy is standard and the answer is unambiguous.

items.q: During a perilunate dislocation, the carpus escapes through a weak area between the radioscaphocapitate and long radiolunate ligaments. What is this area called?
items.e: The space of Poirier is a weak area over the capitolunate joint, between the radioscaphocapitate and long radiolunate ligaments. Perilunate dislocations can pass through it.
items.note: The anatomy and its relationship to perilunate dislocation are supported.

items.q: A patient presents with a fluctuant abscess around the nail fold after a hangnail. Pus is also present beneath the nail plate. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Warm soaks and oral antibiotics alone
Incision and elevation of the nail fold, with partial nail plate removal
items.e: An abscess in acute paronychia requires incision and elevation of the nail fold. Partial nail plate removal is indicated when pus lies beneath the nail plate.
items.note: Accurate, focused single-best-answer question.

items.q: Which incision is preferred for drainage of a felon while reducing the risk of injury to the neurovascular bundles and flexor sheath?
o: A transverse incision across the fingertip pulp
A through-and-through incision from the volar to dorsal surface
A high lateral mid-axial incision on the non-contact side, kept distal to the DIP crease
A longitudinal incision directly over the flexor sheath
items.e: A high lateral mid-axial incision on the non-contact side permits drainage while avoiding the neurovascular bundles and flexor sheath. Fish-mouth and through-and-through incisions should be avoided.
items.note: The described incision and anatomical precautions are supported by the notes.

items.q: A healthcare worker develops burning and tingling in a fingertip followed by clustered clear vesicles on an erythematous base. The pulp is not tense. What is the best management?
o: Incision and drainage, followed by antibiotics
Immediate open debridement of the fingertip
Protective dressing and oral acyclovir if presenting within 48–72 hours
items.e: This is characteristic of herpetic whitlow, which is managed non-operatively with a protective dressing; oral acyclovir may be used when presentation is within 48–72 hours. Incision and drainage is avoided because it can cause secondary bacterial infection.
items.note: The answer is correct, but the original explanation's claim about systemic viraemia and encephalitis is not needed and is an insufficiently secure rationale for the incision warning.

items.q: In pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis, which of the following is the earliest and most sensitive Kanavel sign?
o: The finger is held in slight flexion
Pain on passive extension of the finger
items.e: Pain on passive extension is the earliest and most sensitive of the four Kanavel signs. It occurs along the course of the flexor sheath.
items.note: Clear, supported distinction among the four Kanavel signs.

items.q: A patient has early finger symptoms, equivocal signs of flexor sheath infection, and presentation within 24 hours. Which initial approach is appropriate?
o: IV antibiotics, splinting and elevation, with reassessment within 12–24 hours
Immediate amputation of the affected digit
Incision and drainage of the pulp space
items.e: Early pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis with equivocal signs may be managed initially with IV antibiotics, splinting and elevation. The patient should be reassessed within 12–24 hours, with surgery if there is no improvement.
items.note: The stem specifies the early, equivocal presentation for which this initial approach is supported.

items.q: A newborn has a congenital transverse deficiency of the hand. Which signalling centre and molecule are most closely associated with defects along this developmental axis?
o: Zone of polarising activity (ZPA) — sonic hedgehog
Apical ectodermal ridge (AER) — fibroblast growth factors
items.e: The AER and its FGF signals regulate proximal-distal development. Defects in this axis can cause transverse deficiencies and symbrachydactyly.
items.note: Clear single-best-answer question supported by the notes.

items.q: Failure of which process during weeks 6–8 most directly results in syndactyly?
o: Interdigital tissue apoptosis mediated by bone morphogenetic proteins
SHH signalling from the posterior mesoderm
FGF signalling from the apical ectodermal ridge
Wnt-7a signalling in the dorsal ectoderm
items.e: Digit separation depends on apoptosis of the interdigital tissue, mediated by BMPs. Failure of this process produces syndactyly.
items.note: Accurate timing and mechanism; options are clearly distinguishable.

items.q: In the Oberg-Manske-Tonkin classification, a constriction ring is classified as a:
items.e: OMT classifies a constriction ring as a deformation. Malformations involve abnormal axis formation or differentiation, while dysplasias include conditions such as macrodactyly.
items.note: Correct OMT category and unambiguous options.

items.q: Which is the commonest site of congenital syndactyly?
items.e: The third web space, between the middle and ring fingers, is the commonest site and accounts for about half of cases.
items.note: The commonest-site claim and approximate frequency are supported by the notes.

items.q: A newborn has a rudimentary, pedunculated postaxial digit. Which statement about its classification and management is correct?
o: Temtamy–McKusick type A; excision at about 9–12 months with ligament reconstruction
Temtamy–McKusick type B; suture ligation or surgical excision
Wassel type IV; central wedge resection and combination of both halves
Wassel type VII; pollicisation of the duplicated digit
items.e: A rudimentary pedunculated postaxial digit is Temtamy–McKusick type B. It may be treated by nursery suture ligation or surgical excision; ligation can leave a residual bump or neuroma.
items.note: Classification and management are accurate, and the thumb-duplication options do not fit the stem.

items.q: During fasciectomy for a little-finger PIP flexion contracture, which diseased structure places the digital neurovascular bundle at particular risk by displacing it centrally, superficially and proximally?
items.e: A spiral cord incorporates the spiral band, lateral digital sheet, Grayson ligament and pretendinous band. It displaces the neurovascular bundle centrally, superficially and proximally, making it vulnerable during dissection.
items.note: Accurate, focused single-best-answer question.

items.q: A patient with Dupuytren disease has a 35° MCP joint contracture and a 10° PIP joint contracture. Which statement best reflects usual thresholds for considering intervention?
o: Intervention is generally considered for the MCP contracture, but the PIP contracture is below the usual threshold
Neither contracture meets the usual threshold
Only the PIP contracture meets the usual threshold
Both contractures are below the usual threshold
items.e: An MCP contracture of 30° or more is a usual indication for intervention. PIP contractures are generally considered at about 15–20° or more, so 10° is below that threshold.
items.note: Thresholds and application to the stated contractures are consistent with the notes.

items.q: A young patient has recurrent Dupuytren contracture, aggressive disease and involvement of the overlying skin. Which operation is most appropriate to reduce recurrence?
items.e: Dermofasciectomy removes the diseased fascia and involved overlying skin, which is replaced with a full-thickness skin graft. It is used for recurrent or aggressive disease and has the lowest recurrence among the listed options.
items.note: Indication and recurrence comparison are supported by the notes.

items.q: After injection of collagenase into a Dupuytren cord, what is the usual next step and timing?
o: Begin night extension splinting immediately without manipulation
Manipulate the finger to rupture the cord 24–72 hours later
Repeat the injection after one week before manipulating
items.e: Collagenase enzymatically lyses collagen in the cord. The finger is manipulated 24–72 hours after injection to rupture it; skin tears are a common significant complication during manipulation.
items.note: Timing and next step match the reference notes.

items.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is being considered for shoulder, wrist and finger procedures. Which operative sequence is generally preferred?
o: Finger procedures, then wrist, then shoulder
Operate first on the most deformed joint, regardless of level
items.e: Proximal joints are generally addressed before distal reconstruction so the hand can be positioned in space. The wrist is stabilised before finger reconstruction because wrist deformity can contribute to finger deformity.
items.note: The sequence reflects the standard proximal-to-distal reconstruction principle.

items.q: In rheumatoid arthritis, attritional rupture of the flexor pollicis longus over a scaphoid spur has occurred. Which treatment combination best addresses the lesion and restores thumb function?
o: Excise the spur and reconstruct the tendon with graft or transfer, or fuse the thumb IP joint
Excise the distal ulna and perform extensor tendon transfer
Release the first web space and reconstruct the thumb UCL
items.e: The Mannerfelt lesion is attritional FPL rupture over a volar scaphoid spur. Management includes spur excision and restoring function with tendon graft or transfer, or thumb IP joint fusion.
items.note: The lesion and listed treatment options are standard.

items.q: A patient develops a posterior dislocation soon after primary THA performed through a posterior approach. Which intraoperative measure would have most directly reduced this approach-related risk?
o: Repair of the posterior capsule and short external rotators
Extension of the gluteus medius split proximally
Release of the tensor fasciae latae
items.e: Posterior capsular and short external rotator repair reduces dislocation after the posterior approach; the notes cite about 1% with repair versus 4% without.
items.note: Correct, supported, and has one clear best answer.

items.q: During a direct lateral Hardinge approach, the gluteus medius split is extended well above the greater trochanter tip. Which complication is most specifically associated with this manoeuvre?
o: Sciatic nerve palsy with foot drop
Superior gluteal nerve injury with abductor weakness and Trendelenburg gait
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve injury with meralgia paraesthetica
Femoral nerve injury with quadriceps weakness
items.e: A split extending more than about 5 cm above the greater trochanter tip risks injury to the superior gluteal nerve, causing abductor weakness and a Trendelenburg limp.
items.note: Correct and supported; the threshold and resulting deficit are specified.

items.q: Which statement about the direct anterior approach to THA is correct?
o: Its superficial interval is between sartorius and tensor fasciae latae, both supplied by the femoral nerve.
Its deep interval is between rectus femoris and gluteus medius, both supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.
The ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery may require ligation.
Its characteristic sensory complication is injury to the superior gluteal nerve.
items.e: The ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery is encountered during the approach and may require ligation. The superficial and deep intervals are between muscles supplied by different nerves, and the characteristic sensory complication is lateral femoral cutaneous nerve symptoms.
items.note: As written, A, B, and C are all correct; revised A and B to make the item single-best-answer.

items.q: A surgeon chooses the Watson-Jones anterolateral approach for a primary THA. Which interval is used?
o: Tensor fasciae latae and gluteus medius
Gluteus maximus and short external rotators
items.e: The Watson-Jones approach passes between tensor fasciae latae and gluteus medius. Both muscles are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, so this is not a true internervous plane.
items.note: Correct, supported, and has one clear best answer.

items.q: During acetabular exposure, an anterior retractor is placed too medially over the anterior acetabular rim. Which structures are particularly at risk?
o: Sciatic nerve and superior gluteal vessels
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve and ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery
items.e: The femoral neurovascular structures lie anteriorly and can be injured by an anterior retractor placed too medially over the acetabular rim.
items.note: Correct and supported by the approach-related anatomy.

items.q: Which approach is most associated with good femoral exposure and preservation of the abductors, but also carries an approach-specific risk of sciatic nerve injury?
items.e: The posterior approach splits gluteus maximus and releases the short external rotators and posterior capsule; it preserves the abductors and provides good femoral exposure, but the sciatic nerve is at risk.
items.note: Correct, supported, and has one clear best answer.

items.q: In mechanical-alignment TKA, the distal femoral cut is planned perpendicular to the femoral mechanical axis. An intramedullary guide references the anatomical axis. At what valgus angle is the distal femoral cut typically set relative to that anatomical axis?
items.e: The anatomical and mechanical femoral axes differ by about 5–7°. Setting the distal femoral cut at this valgus angle to the anatomical axis makes it perpendicular to the mechanical axis.
items.note: Accurately tests the standard distal femoral cut angle.

items.q: After the tibial and distal femoral cuts, both the flexion and extension gaps are tight. Which adjustment best addresses this pattern?
items.e: The tibial cut contributes to both the flexion and extension gaps, so additional tibial resection opens both. Distal femoral resection affects only the extension gap.
items.note: The gap pattern and proposed correction are clear and unambiguous.

items.q: A TKA has an elevated joint line because of excessive distal femoral resection combined with a thick insert. Which complication is associated with this?
items.e: Excessive joint-line elevation is associated with mid-flexion instability and can also cause pseudo-patella baja and patellofemoral problems.
items.note: The complication is correctly linked to joint-line elevation.

items.q: A patient with severe valgus and a fixed flexion contracture undergoes TKA. Which complication is specifically associated with correction of this deformity, and what manoeuvre may reduce the risk?
o: Femoral tracker-pin fracture; use unicortical pins
Peroneal nerve palsy; flex the knee
items.e: Correcting severe valgus with a flexion contracture can stretch the peroneal nerve. Flexing the knee may reduce this stretch.
items.note: The complication and risk-reduction manoeuvre are supported.

items.q: During correction of a varus knee, which step should be performed before releasing the medial soft tissues?
o: Remove medial tibial and femoral osteophytes
items.e: Medial osteophytes should be removed first in a varus knee, before proceeding to medial soft-tissue releases.
items.note: Tests the standard initial step in medial balancing of a varus knee.

items.q: After bone cuts, the flexion gap is tight but the extension gap is balanced. Which is an appropriate adjustment?
items.e: Isolated flexion-gap tightness can be addressed by downsizing the femoral component. Other options described for this pattern include increasing tibial slope or releasing the PCL in a cruciate-retaining knee.
items.note: The selected option is an appropriate adjustment for isolated flexion-gap tightness.

items.q: Which statement best describes kinematic alignment in TKA?
o: Both bone cuts are perpendicular to the mechanical axes, with balance achieved through soft-tissue releases
The pre-arthritic joint is resurfaced to restore native joint lines and limb alignment, with minimal releases
The joint line is set at 3° varus while the limb is kept neutral
The tibial component is aligned to the medial third of the tibial tubercle
items.e: Kinematic alignment aims to resurface the pre-arthritic joint and restore native joint lines and HKA alignment, generally with minimal releases. The other options describe mechanical alignment, historical anatomical alignment, and a tibial rotational landmark, respectively.
items.note: The tested alignment philosophy is clearly distinguished from the alternatives.

items.q: A patient with a painful total knee arthroplasty has a sinus tract that communicates with the joint. Under the 2018 ICM definition, how should this finding be interpreted?
o: It is a major criterion and establishes infection
It contributes 3 points and requires a total score of at least 6
It contributes 2 points and requires confirmatory intraoperative histology
It is not diagnostic unless serum CRP is also elevated
items.e: A sinus tract communicating with the joint is a major criterion for PJI under the 2018 ICM definition; either major criterion establishes infection.
items.note: Correct, direct application of a 2018 ICM major criterion.

items.q: A patient undergoing evaluation for chronic PJI has serum CRP of 15 mg/L, ESR of 35 mm/h and synovial WBC of 3,500 cells/µL. What is the preoperative ICM classification?
o: Inconclusive until two cultures are positive
items.e: These findings score 2 points for CRP, 1 for ESR and 3 for synovial WBC, giving a total of 6. A preoperative score of 6 or more indicates infection.
items.note: Correct score calculation and classification using the stated chronic-PJI thresholds.

items.q: Within six weeks of hip arthroplasty, which set of values is consistent with the higher acute postoperative thresholds cited in the 2018 ICM framework?
o: CRP over 10 mg/L, synovial WBC over 3,000 cells/µL, PMN over 80%
CRP over 100 mg/L, synovial WBC over about 10,000 cells/µL, PMN over about 90%
CRP over 30 mg/L, synovial WBC over 1,500 cells/µL, PMN over 50%
CRP over 860 mg/L, synovial WBC over 30,000 cells/µL, PMN over 80%
items.e: In the early postoperative period, surgical inflammation raises these markers, so higher thresholds are used: CRP over 100 mg/L, synovial WBC over about 10,000 cells/µL and PMN over about 90%.
items.note: Matches the early postoperative thresholds specified in the reference notes.

items.q: A painful arthroplasty has a preoperative ICM score of 4. Which approach is appropriate to complete the assessment?
o: Classify the joint as not infected without further assessment
Classify the joint as infected because any score above 3 is diagnostic
Add relevant intraoperative findings to the score
Repeat serum ESR and CRP until the score reaches 6
items.e: A preoperative score of 2–5 is in the possibly infected range. Intraoperative findings are added to help resolve the diagnosis.
items.note: Correctly tests how to proceed with an inconclusive preoperative score.

items.q: Which histological finding meets the 2018 ICM intraoperative criterion for positive histology?
o: More than 5 neutrophils per high-power field in 5 or more fields
More than 5 neutrophils per high-power field in a single field
At least 5 neutrophils per high-power field in 3 fields
Any neutrophils seen in at least 5 fields
items.e: The ICM intraoperative histology criterion is more than 5 neutrophils per high-power field in 5 or more fields; this finding contributes 3 points.
items.note: Accurately states the specified histological threshold and field count.

items.q: Which wear mechanism is most common in metal-on-polyethylene arthroplasty?
items.e: Adhesive wear is the commonest mechanism in metal-on-polyethylene bearings: polymer transfers to the counterface and is then pulled away.
items.note: The mechanism and the comparison with fatigue wear are supported by the notes.

items.q: For conventional polyethylene, linear wear is measured at 0.12 mm/year on serial radiographs. Which statement best describes the significance of this finding?
o: It is below the usual osteolysis threshold
It exceeds the approximate osteolysis threshold
items.e: The approximate osteolysis threshold for conventional polyethylene is 0.1 mm/year of linear wear. Linear wear describes head penetration into the liner, whereas volumetric wear reflects particle load.
items.note: The threshold and distinction between linear and volumetric wear are accurately stated.

items.q: A highly cross-linked polyethylene liner is thermally treated above its melting point to eliminate free radicals. Which trade-off is associated with this treatment?
o: It preserves crystallinity but leaves more free radicals
It reduces crystallinity, fatigue strength and fracture toughness
It increases free radicals without affecting mechanical properties
It prevents cross-linking of the polyethylene chains
items.e: Remelting eliminates free radicals but reduces crystallinity, fatigue strength and fracture toughness. Annealing below the melting point better preserves mechanical properties but leaves some free radicals.
items.note: The stem identifies remelting, and the stated trade-off is correct.

items.q: A patient develops tibial osteolysis after total knee arthroplasty with a modular polyethylene insert. Which wear pattern can contribute to this finding in addition to wear at the articulating surface?
o: Backside wear from micromotion against the tibial tray
Fluid-film wear between the insert and tray
Wear from ceramic particles at the femoral component
Adhesive wear at a modular metal taper
items.e: Micromotion between a modular insert and the tibial tray can cause backside wear, which contributes to tibial osteolysis.
items.note: Backside wear is a recognised contributor to tibial osteolysis in modular TKA.

items.q: During revision of a total hip arthroplasty, a fractured ceramic femoral head is encountered. Which bearing choice is recommended for the revision, assuming the taper is suitable?
o: A metal head, because ceramic debris is harmless to metal
A ceramic head, because ceramic particles can rapidly wear a metal head
An oxidised zirconium head, because its surface cannot be breached
A larger metal-on-metal head, to reduce volumetric wear
items.e: Revision to a ceramic head is recommended because retained ceramic particles can cause catastrophic wear of a metal head. The procedure also includes full synovectomy; a damaged trunnion requires a new taper sleeve.
items.note: The recommended bearing choice and the risk from retained ceramic debris are correctly stated.

items.q: Which description best explains why ceramic-on-ceramic bearings can achieve very low wear?
o: They rely on boundary lubrication and have soft, conforming surfaces
Their hardness and wettability support fluid-film lubrication
They generate no particles under any conditions
Their low wear depends on deliberate edge loading
items.e: Ceramics are hard, scratch-resistant and highly wettable, favouring fluid-film lubrication. Ceramic-on-ceramic has the lowest wear among the listed bearing types, although ceramic bearings can still fracture or squeak.
items.note: The explanation matches the stated bearing properties and avoids claiming zero wear.

items.q: A patient with a painful THA is being considered for revision because serial radiographs show progressive loosening. What should be done before proceeding with revision?
o: Obtain ESR/CRP, with aspiration if indicated, to exclude infection
Order a bone scan and revise if uptake is present
Measure metal ions in every patient
Proceed directly to revision if the components are migrated
items.e: Infection should be excluded before revision of any painful or failing arthroplasty. ESR/CRP and, when indicated, aspiration are part of the work-up; bone-scan findings for loosening are non-specific.
items.note: Correctly tests the infection work-up before revision.

items.q: A revision THA radiograph shows superior acetabular migration of 4 cm, a breached Kohler line, severe ischial lysis and a deficient rim involving more than 60% of its circumference. Which Paprosky type and reconstruction best fit this defect?
o: IIB; jumbo cup with particulate graft
IIIA; jumbo cup with porous metal augments
IIIB; cup-cage or custom triflange reconstruction
items.e: These findings indicate Paprosky type IIIB, characterised by major rim loss, non-supportive columns and a breached Kohler line. A cup-cage or custom triflange are among the listed reconstruction options.
items.note: The findings and reconstruction match Paprosky IIIB.

items.q: During revision THA, a well-fixed femoral stem and its cement mantle must be removed while preserving the remaining bone. Which approach is specifically suited to this situation?
items.e: An extended trochanteric osteotomy facilitates removal of well-fixed stems or cement and can help correct proximal deformity. The osteotomy is typically about 10–15 cm and is fixed with cables.
items.note: ETO is the relevant femoral exposure and extraction technique.

items.q: On serial radiographs after THA, which finding supports bone ingrowth and a stable uncemented femoral stem rather than loosening?
o: Pedestal formation at the stem tip
Progressive radiolucent lines wider than 2 mm
items.e: Spot welds indicate bone ingrowth and support stable fixation. Pedestal formation around the distal tip of an uncemented stem is associated with loosening.
items.note: Spot welds are the radiographic sign of bone ingrowth.

items.q: Which finding constitutes definite femoral stem loosening under the Harris criteria for a cemented stem?
o: Lucency over 50–100% of the bone-cement interface
A continuous radiolucent line around the entire cement mantle
A non-progressive radiolucent line measuring less than 2 mm
items.e: Harris criteria classify stem migration, cement fracture or stem fracture as definite loosening. A continuous line around the entire cement mantle is probable loosening, while lucency over 50–100% of the interface is possible loosening.
items.note: The Harris criteria classify migration as definite loosening.

items.q: In the AORI classification of bone loss at revision TKA, both femoral condyles or tibial plateaus have damaged metaphyseal bone. Which type and reconstruction are most appropriate?
o: Type 1; cement with or without screws
Type 2A; metal augments for one condyle or plateau
Type 2B; augments with cones or sleeves
Type 3; standard components without metaphyseal reconstruction
items.e: AORI type 2B describes damaged metaphysis involving both condyles or plateaus. Reconstruction commonly uses augments together with metaphyseal cones or sleeves.
items.note: The bilateral metaphyseal defect is AORI type 2B.

items.q: A 76-year-old with a three-part proximal humerus fracture undergoes reverse total shoulder arthroplasty. Which factor is the single absolute requirement for this reconstruction to function?
o: A functioning deltoid and intact axillary nerve
A glenoid with no posterior erosion
items.e: Reverse arthroplasty depends on a functioning deltoid, supplied by an intact axillary nerve, to achieve elevation. Tuberosity repair can improve rotation and elevation but is not the single absolute requirement.
items.note: The stem and answer correctly identify the key functional requirement for reverse arthroplasty.

items.q: On axial CT, a glenoid has a biconcave articular surface, posterior erosion and posterior humeral-head subluxation. Which Walch type best describes this morphology?
items.e: Walch B2 morphology is characterised by a biconcave glenoid with posterior erosion and posterior humeral-head subluxation. B1 has posterior narrowing and sclerosis without the characteristic biconcavity.
items.note: The morphology is characteristic of Walch B2.

items.q: Which is the most common long-term failure mode of anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty?
items.e: Glenoid component loosening is the commonest long-term failure of anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty. Eccentric loading by a superiorly migrating humeral head can produce the rocking-horse phenomenon.
items.note: The tested long-term failure mode and the distinction from reverse arthroplasty complications are sound.

items.q: A patient with cuff tear arthropathy has a painful reverse shoulder arthroplasty. Radiographs show erosion of the inferior scapular neck where the humeral cup contacts it during adduction. Which classification is used to grade this finding?
items.e: Scapular notching after reverse shoulder arthroplasty is graded using the Sirveaux classification. Inferior glenosphere placement, inferior tilt and lateralisation are among the measures that can reduce its occurrence.
items.note: The described radiographic finding is scapular notching, graded by Sirveaux.

items.q: A man develops a low-grade shoulder prosthetic infection. Initial cultures show no growth, but clinical suspicion remains; the organism of concern is slow-growing. How long should cultures be held?
items.e: Cutibacterium acnes is the commonest organism in shoulder periprosthetic joint infection and may grow slowly. Cultures should be held for 14 days.
items.note: The incubation period matches the reference notes for suspected C. acnes infection.

items.q: A patient has a massive chronic rotator-cuff tear, an acromiohumeral interval of 4 mm and humeral-head collapse. Which Hamada grade is this?
items.e: Hamada grade 5 includes humeral-head collapse. Grades 3 and 4 describe acetabularisation and glenohumeral arthritis, respectively.
items.note: Humeral-head collapse is the distinguishing feature of Hamada grade 5.

items.q: A 62-year-old woman has activity-related medial knee pain. Weight-bearing radiographs show bone-on-bone medial compartment osteoarthritis, with preserved lateral compartment and correctable varus. She has a stable knee and an intact ACL. Which procedure is the best option?
items.e: Isolated medial compartment disease, correctable deformity and a functionally intact ACL are key features supporting medial UKA. The other compartments are not radiographically involved.

items.q: A patient with medial compartment osteoarthritis is being assessed for medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty. Which finding is a contraindication to this procedure?
items.e: A functionally deficient ACL can lead to abnormal knee kinematics and failure of a medial UKA. Correctable deformity, preserved lateral cartilage and isolated full-thickness medial disease are compatible with UKA.

items.q: A 58-year-old active patient has symptomatic lateral compartment osteoarthritis with valgus alignment. The medial compartment is preserved, and the deformity arises predominantly from the distal femur. Which joint-preserving procedure is most appropriate?
items.e: A distal femoral varus osteotomy corrects valgus arising from the distal femur and shifts load away from the diseased lateral compartment. The level of the deformity guides the choice of osteotomy.

items.q: During medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy, a fracture propagates through the lateral cortical hinge. Which complication is most directly associated with this event?
items.e: A lateral hinge fracture can destabilize the osteotomy and allow loss of correction. Maintaining an intact lateral cortical hinge helps preserve stability.

items.q: A patient with a mobile-bearing medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty develops sudden pain after rising from a low chair. Radiographs show the polyethylene insert displaced from between the femoral and tibial components. What is this complication?
items.e: Displacement of the mobile polyethylene insert is bearing dislocation, a characteristic complication of mobile-bearing UKA. It commonly presents with acute pain and restricted movement.

items.q: Which radiographic study is most useful for planning the correction in a patient being considered for a high tibial osteotomy for varus knee osteoarthritis?
o: Merchant view of the patellofemoral joint
items.e: A weight-bearing long-leg radiograph demonstrates the mechanical axis and helps localize the deformity and plan the amount of correction.

items.q: Which statement about medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty is correct?
o: It is intended to replace both tibiofemoral compartments
It preserves the cruciate ligaments when they are functional
It is indicated for inflammatory arthritis affecting multiple compartments
items.e: UKA replaces the diseased compartment while preserving the unaffected compartments and, when functional, the cruciate ligaments. Multicompartment inflammatory arthritis is not an appropriate indication.

items.q: During examination of an ACL-deficient knee, anterior drawer laxity is assessed at 90° of flexion. Which ACL bundle is the primary restraint to anterior tibial translation in this position?
items.e: The anteromedial bundle tightens in flexion and is the primary restraint to anterior tibial translation at 90°. The posterolateral bundle is tight in extension and contributes to rotational restraint.
items.note: Accurate, supported and has one clear answer.

items.q: A patient with an acute ACL injury has MRI evidence of a pivot-shift bone-bruise pattern. Which combination of sites is most characteristic?
o: Medial femoral condyle and anteromedial tibial plateau
Lateral femoral condyle at the sulcus terminalis and posterolateral tibial plateau
Lateral femoral condyle and anteromedial tibial plateau
items.e: Pivot-shift injury commonly produces opposing bone bruises on the lateral femoral condyle at the sulcus terminalis and the posterolateral tibial plateau.
items.note: Accurate, supported and has one clear answer.

items.q: Which clinical test is the most sensitive examination for ACL insufficiency?
items.e: The Lachman test, performed with the knee flexed about 20–30°, is the most sensitive clinical test for ACL injury. The pivot-shift test is the most specific.
items.note: The clinical-test qualifier makes the intended comparison clear; the answer is supported.

items.q: In chronic ACL deficiency, which meniscal injury becomes more likely as the meniscus assumes a secondary restraint role?
o: Anterior horn tear of the lateral meniscus
Posterior horn tear of the medial meniscus
Posterior horn tear of the lateral meniscus
Anterior horn tear of the medial meniscus
items.e: With chronic ACL deficiency, posterior horn tears of the medial meniscus become more frequent because it acts as a secondary restraint. In acute ACL injuries, the lateral meniscus is more commonly torn.
items.note: Accurate and distinguishes the chronic pattern from the acute association.

items.q: A young athlete has an ACL rupture but marked swelling, restricted extension and poor quadriceps control. If reconstruction is planned, what is the preferred timing principle?
o: Proceed immediately, regardless of range of motion
Wait until swelling resolves and full extension and quadriceps control return
Wait until the athlete has completed a season of sport
Reconstruct only after a recurrent meniscal tear develops
items.e: Reconstruction is generally timed after swelling has settled and full extension and quadriceps control have returned. This prehabilitation approach reduces the risk of arthrofibrosis.
items.note: The timing principle is supported and the clinical findings make the intended answer clear.

items.q: Compared with a BPTB graft, which commonly used ACL autograft has soft-tissue healing and may cause weakness in deep knee flexion?
items.e: A quadrupled hamstring autograft heals through soft-tissue incorporation and can cause hamstring weakness, particularly in deep flexion. A quadriceps tendon graft may also heal as soft tissue when used without a bone block, so the added hamstring-specific feature makes this a single-best-answer question.
items.note: The original stem is ambiguous because quadriceps tendon grafts can also have soft-tissue healing and less anterior knee pain.
